Lukas pulled over, unplugged the phone from the charger and looked at the clock. The tank was full, but a flat parcel was waiting at the post office, and Lukas did not know if it was open. "Hey phone, is the post office on Mill Street open now?" The assistant said it was open until five. Lukas thought for a moment. "Good. Remind me to check the mailbox every Monday at nine, and tell me when a parcel comes." The assistant said it had made a reminder for every Monday at nine, called check the mailbox. Lukas said thank you, plugged the phone back in and drove to Mill Street.

Bo is a grandparent who plans the school lunches for two grandchildren. On Sunday, Bo said to the kitchen speaker, "Please plan this week's lunches and make a shopping list from them." The speaker gave five easy lunches, one for each school day, and put everything needed on a list. Bo wanted to hear it clear and slow, so the speaker read it out. It had bread, cheese, apples and a dozen eggs. Then Bo remembered something. "One of the children cannot eat nuts. Reset the plan and leave out the peanut butter." The speaker reset the week with no nuts at all, put egg salad on Tuesday instead, and told Bo the list had changed. Bo nodded and went to find a coat for the shops.

Many people take medicine at set times, and a reminder helps them not to forget a dose. A dose is the amount you take each time, such as one pill with water. Doctors say how long to continue, and some medicines work best if you drink a full glass of water with them. People say, remind me to take my pill at eight every morning, or move my reminder to nine. They also change doctor's appointments. They say, book me in for next Friday, or make it the final slot of the day. Many people put a star next to the visits they must not miss. Simple words and a clear time are enough.

Someone wants to know how many days are left until a date.
how many days till friday
days until my birthday?
how mny days to christmas
How long until the big match on the ninth? I want to cheer for my team.
I have a bike wheel to pick up on the twentieth, so how many days is that from today?
The party is on the fourteenth at six sharp, so how many days do I still have?
Could you please tell me how many sleeps are left until the holiday?

Someone wants the phone to start recording a video.
start recording
record a video
start the camra
Is the camera working? Please film this.
My dad is about to laugh at his birthday cake, so start a video now.
Can you start a video? The radio is playing our song and I want to keep it.
I would like to film the dog in the garden, could you begin recording, please?

A huge storm hit the town, and the lights went out at Keisha's house. Keisha, a retired teacher, sat in the dark with a cold cup of tea and spoke to the phone. "The power is off and there is ice on the road outside. How long will it be out?" The assistant looked up the power company and said the repairs would take about two hours, maybe more if the ice got thicker. "Then I need more light," said Keisha. The assistant turned on the phone's torch at half brightness to save the battery, and said it would continue to check the power company every ten minutes. Keisha lit two candles, put on a thick coat and waited.

Person: Can you speak the news while I work? My hands are full of soil.
Assistant: Of course. Which news would you like: local, sports or world?
Person: Local, and not too much. Three headlines, fewer than yesterday.
Assistant: Here are three. The town is planning a new bridge. A school fair is on Saturday. A bakery is closing for repairs.
Person: Is there any news about the garden show in September?
Assistant: I can't find anything about it yet. I can look again tomorrow if you like.
Person: Yes please. I want my neat rows of tulips to be ready.

Imran sat in the dorm room with an empty stomach and a lecture at seven. The food Imran had ordered online was late. "I'm starving, and it has been an hour," Imran said to the phone. The assistant understood and checked the order. It said the driver was two streets away and would arrive in about five minutes. Then Imran saw that the flat number on the screen was wrong. "Can you fix that? It's flat twelve, not twenty-one." The assistant changed the address on the order and sent a short note to the driver. A few minutes later someone knocked on the door. The food was still hot, and Imran made it to the lecture on time.

Person: I can't stand these phones. My girl has homework and I need some help.
Assistant: I can help. What would you like me to do for her homework?
Person: Remind her to read. Every day.
Assistant: Sure. What time should I remind her?
Person: After school. In twenty minutes? No, I mean at four o'clock.
Assistant: Got it. A daily reminder at four o'clock to read. Is that right?
Person: Yes, thank you. That was easy.

Heating keeps a home warm. A thermostat is a small dial or screen that tells the heater what temperature you want. When people feel cold, they say, make it warmer, or turn it up two degrees. When the room is too hot, they say, lower it a little. A weak radiator may need more time to warm a big room, so some people start the heating an hour early. Many thermostats record the temperature all day, so you can see when the house was coldest. Cooking with an oven or a microwave can warm a kitchen a little, but only the heating warms the whole home.

Ayita ran a small chocolate shop on Palm Street, and the morning was slow. While waiting for the first customers, Ayita said to the speaker on the counter, "Read me the local headlines and tell me if the street market is open on Saturday." The speaker read three headlines. One was about a new bakery, one was about road work, and one was about a school choir. Then it said the street market would open on Saturday at eight. Ayita smiled. Friendly neighbours often come in to chat, and now there was plenty to talk about. When the first customer walked in, Ayita said, "Did you hear about the new bakery?"

Yuki was kneeling in the garden with muddy hands, drawing up a plan to design a new flower bed. The soil was dry and hard, and the tablet on the bench was too far to touch. "Make the text bigger and read my notes out loud," Yuki said. The tablet made the letters twice as large and read the notes in a slow voice: tulips by the fence, herbs near the door, water twice a week. Then Yuki remembered the time. "And remind me to take my pill at noon." The tablet said the reminder was set. Yuki kept digging and listening to the notes, and did not need to wipe a single finger.

Remy had just moved to the city and found a small pool on the roof of the building. It was full of fallen leaves, and the water looked cold. From the roof, the mountain in the distance was lovely, but Remy wanted a swim. "Tell me the water temperature and print the cleaning schedule," Remy said to the phone. The phone said the water was eighteen degrees and that the pool was cleaned every Thursday. A moment later the printer in the lobby began to print the schedule. Remy picked up the page, saw that the pump would run until noon, and decided to wait a day for a warmer swim.

name: log_sleep_night
does: Writes down how a night of sleep went, such as a broken night, so the user can see patterns over time.
inputs: the night, how many hours were slept, and any notes, like a late supper of corn or a night on a ship
people say:
- I slept badly last night, write it down
- log that I woke up three times
- note that I only got five hours
- remember that I had a bad night after the late dinner
- save how I slept, please

name: laundry_ready_alert
does: Tells the user when a washer or dryer cycle is finished and the clothes are ready, and keeps a file of past cycles.
inputs: which machine, and whether the clothes are muddy from planting tomatoes or just everyday wear
people say:
- tell me when the wash is done
- is my dryer finished yet?
- ping me when the clothes are ready
- let me know when the laundry stops spinning
- I'm going out, shout when the machine is done

Someone wants a recipe made bigger for more people.
double it
Scale it up
make it bigger
Can you write the amounts again for eight people instead of four?
I am cooking the red lentil soup for twelve guests, so please make the recipe feed three times as many.
I need enough sauce to dress the salad for ten, how much of each thing?
The recipe says four servings, but we are six. Can you change the numbers?

Someone wants milk put on the shopping list.
add milk to my list
put eggs on the list
need bread on the shoping list
We are out of milk, can you put it on the list?
The main thing I need this week is rice, so please add it to my grocery list.
My baking class is tonight and I need flour, so write it on the list.
Put sugar on my list, I want to mix a cake tomorrow.

A baby monitor lets parents hear or see a baby from another room. A small microphone near the cot picks up sounds, and a speaker or phone plays them. Some monitors have a silver light that shows how loud the room is. Babies grow fast, and the days seem to fly by, so parents like a plan: feeding times, nap times and bedtime. They set reminders, like feed the baby at three. When the plan changes, people say, move the nap to two o'clock, or make the monitor louder, or turn it down a little. Short, quiet words work best, so a sleeping baby is not woken up.

name: make_my_drink
does: Starts the coffee machine or kettle so a creamy cup of coffee or tea is ready when the user comes back from the mailbox or wakes up.
inputs: the drink, how strong, how sweet, and whether to fold in milk or cream
people say:
- make me a strong coffee
- I need a cup of tea, not too sweet
- can you start the coffee machine?
- a latte with extra milk, please
- I'm up, get my morning drink going

Thabo woke up to a faint dripping sound and a wet patch near the kitchen wall. Half asleep, Thabo spoke to the home assistant. "Good morning. Could you please check the water use in the house? I think there might be a leak, and I would hate for the bill to be huge this month." The assistant connected to the water meter and said that water was running even though nothing was on. It pointed to the pipe near the main tap. Thabo remembered the chicken thawing in the sink, but that was not the problem. The assistant offered to close the main valve and Thabo said yes. The dripping stopped. Then Thabo asked it to find a plumber for the afternoon.

Sports fans like to follow matches and scores. A score shows how many points each team has. People ask, what's the score? or tell me when the game starts. Players train to run a longer distance or get stronger, and many keep notes about their training. When a new season begins, teams play on set days, and fans ask for reminders. Sometimes the plan changes, so people say, hang on, move my reminder to eight, or tell me when my team is winning. A short, clear request works best: the team, the day and the time.

A washing machine cleans clothes with water and soap. Before you start, you choose a program, the water temperature and the size of the load. A small load needs less water than a big one. While it runs, the screen shows how much time is left, and people ask, how long is left on the wash? When it stops, they get the clothes out and put them in the dryer or hang them up. If a stain is left on a shirt, people say, wash it again, or use a hotter wash. Many also ask to get a message when the machine finishes.

name: send_invites
does: Sends an invitation for a party or a breakfast gathering to the guests on a list.
inputs: who to invite, the date and time, the place, and any note, like for guests who travel a long way or need to bring heavy chairs
people say:
- invite everyone from my list to Saturday's party
- send out the invitations for mum's sixtieth
- tell the guests it starts at six
- ask Tom and Ana to come to the barbecue
- let my friends know about the party on the tenth
- can you message the whole family about Sunday?

Eleanor grabbed a bag and ran for the door. A plane was leaving in two hours, and the electricity bill was due tomorrow. "Excuse me, could you please pay the electricity bill today? I will be away for a week and I do not want to pay a late fee." The assistant said the bill was sixty-two dollars and paid it from the usual account. It sent a receipt to the phone. Eleanor had also been getting constant reminder messages about the bill, so Eleanor asked the assistant to reset them for next month. The assistant did that and wished Eleanor a good trip.

Cyclists use a bike computer or a phone to track a ride. It shows the distance, the speed and how long the ride took. People use it to plan a route, find a quiet road, or compare today's ride with last week's. A great ride might be longer or faster, but it can also just be fun. Some people carry a bag with a few pounds of tools and food, and they ask for the weather before they start. To change things, people say, show me a flatter route, or make the ride shorter, or tell me when I have gone ten miles.

Oksana was a driver, and the day began with snow. Parked outside a cafe, Oksana opened the phone and asked the home printer a question. "Is there paper left? I need the forms printed before I get home, but only half of them." The printer said there were only a few sheets in the tray and the black ink was low. The assistant offered to print half of the forms, ten pages, and add paper to the shopping list. "Yes, please." By the time Oksana got home, the pages were waiting on the table, and dinner was warm in the oven.

name: label_moving_box
does: Writes a label for a moving box and holds a list of what is inside it.
inputs: the room the box belongs to, what is inside, like a lemon squeezer and two pans, and how soon it will be needed, so urgent boxes are not unpacked late
people say:
- label this box kitchen
- put on the list that box five has the plates
- remember what's in the blue box
- make a tag for the bedroom stuff
- I need to know which box has the kettle

Sofia finished the morning in the garden and came into a living room full of hard sun. "Close the living room blinds, please, but do not close the bedroom curtains. I don't want it dark upstairs." The assistant closed the blinds downstairs and left the bedroom ones open. Sofia said, "That sofa was expensive, and I don't want the sun to fade it. And don't forget to open them again at five." The assistant said it would open the living room blinds at five o'clock. A person walking past on the street waved at the garden, and Sofia waved back, glad the room was cool.

name: remember_birthday
does: Saves a person's birthday to the user's account and reminds the user a full week before, in time to buy a card or a gift.
inputs: the person's name, the date, and an optional note, like a gift they hinted at
people say:
- remember my mum's birthday is June 4th
- don't let me forget Sam's birthday
- save Aunt Rosa's birthday, she was born on 12 October
- tell me a week before Dad's birthday
- note that Lena loves tea and add her birthday on the 20th

Someone wants fewer notifications from a social media app.
fewer alerts please
Half as many notifications, please.
I'm tired of the buzzing, turn the alerts down.
I don't care about every like, just tell me about messages.
Can you send me one summary a day instead of all the alerts?
My phone keeps buzzing on the beach and I want less of it.
Could you please cut my notifications to the important ones only, since I get far too many?

Arithmetic is the plain work with numbers: putting them together, taking one away, making groups of equal size, and sharing. People use it when they pay, cook or plan. If a bill is big, they might ask the assistant, what is forty plus twenty-five? or take ten from sixty. For equal sharing, they say, split ninety between three. When a long sum gets confusing, they ask the assistant to restart with the first number. A teacher gives a lesson on each of these, but in everyday life people just use quick words such as plus, minus, times and shared by.

Person: turn on the sprinker for ten minutes
Assistant: Which one? There are two zones, the front and the back.
Person: front please, the flowers by the shop door
Assistant: Done. The front sprinkler is on for ten minutes.
Person: great, they looked so pretty last june and i want them to bloom again
Assistant: Would you like me to water them every morning?
Person: yes, but skip the rainy days. i forgot yesterday because i did not sleep well
Assistant: Understood. Every morning at seven, except when it rains.

Francesca had a dream of visiting Japan, and today the ticket page showed a price in dollars. Francesca was not good with phones, so Francesca spoke slowly to the assistant. "How many euros is fifty dollars?" Then Francesca stopped. "No, wait, I mean pounds, not euros." The assistant said that was fine and gave the answer for pounds: fifty dollars was about forty pounds today. Under a clean blue sky, Francesca sat on a bench in the park and smiled. "That is not so bad," said Francesca. The assistant offered to say the number again if the rate changed, and Francesca said yes.

Someone wants to be reminded to take a coat when leaving the house.
Remind me to take my coat
coat reminder at 7
Remind me about my coat and my keys when I leave.
Could you nudge me before I go out to grab my coat, and tell me the weather?
I often forget my coat, so tell me before I leave.
Ping me at eight about the coat and the umbrella.
Please ask me about my coat each morning, and restart the reminder if I snooze it.

The kitchen was loud, with constant noise from the pans. Pilar was a cook, and a call with the owner was about to start. With flour on both hands, Pilar spoke to the phone. "Join meeting." The assistant opened the call, but the screen asked for a password. "What is the password?" the assistant asked. Pilar said it was in an email. The assistant found the email, read out the number, and typed it in. Then the call began. Pilar put the phone on the shelf and tried to follow the plan while the onions cooked.

Dragan was in the garden, standing by the little wooden bridge over the pond, when the laptop on the bench froze. The wireless link had dropped and the screen was stuck. Muddy hands made typing hard. "Restart laptop," Dragan said. The assistant warned that the battery was at eight percent and asked if that was okay. "Yes, go on." The laptop restarted, the wireless came back, and the screen woke up. Dragan carried it inside to the charger and sat down with a cup of tea.

Remy, a retired teacher, was about to fly to see a grandchild. The bag was by the door, and a bottle of wine for the host sat on top. "Could you please turn on the cameras and the alarm? I will be away for a week, and I think I left the back window open." The assistant switched on the cameras and the alarm and said the back window sensor showed it was open. Remy hurried to shut it, then said, "Thank you. Please send me a message if the motion sensor sees anything." The assistant said it would. Remy locked the door and called a taxi.

Sigrid did not trust new gadgets, but walked up the hill behind the house and had an idea for a poem. The page in the pocket was loose and the pencil was gone. "I would like to say something and have you write it down, please, because I always forget my ideas by the time I get home." The assistant said it was ready. Sigrid said the first lines of the poem, slowly. The assistant saved them as a voice note and a text note called Hill poem. Sigrid smiled. "Can you read it back?" The assistant did, and the lines sounded just right.

Rain poured down on the bus stop and the wind was bitter. Pooja, a student with a heavy bag, wrote the address on a napkin and then spoke to the phone. "Book me a taxi to the library, but not a shared one. And I don't want to be picked up at the front gate, it is closed." The assistant asked where to pick up, and Pooja said the side door on Green Street. It booked a private taxi to that corner and said the car would arrive in six minutes. Pooja put the napkin in a pocket and waited under the roof.

Someone wants to know what a price is in their own money.
How much is that in dollars?
The sign says forty euros, is that a lot for me?
I wish I knew what this costs at home.
A lawn mower here is three hundred pounds, what is that in dollars?
The tag says twenty-five francs. Is that mild or expensive for me?
I wonder what the pound is worth today.
Could you tell me what this costs back home? I can't work it out.

Someone wants to send a text to one friend, not to the whole group.
Text Anna, not the group chat
Message only Tom, not everyone
Send this to Mia alone: I'll be late. Don't put it in the family chat.
Tell Sam I'm unpacking boxes, but don't tell the others.
Write to Jo that the magazine arrived, please don't post it in the group.
Text my brother, but keep it short, I'm comfortable with a few words.
Please message Lee privately, and make sure it doesn't go to the book club chat.

Haruto turned on the kitchen tap and the water came out brown. Haruto was not good with technology and had learned a lesson: ask the phone first. "Call plumber," said Haruto. The assistant said there were two plumbers nearby and asked, "Do you want the nearest one or the cheapest?" Haruto said the nearest. The assistant booked a visit for four o'clock and sent the time to the phone. "Shall I remind you an hour before?" Haruto said yes, closed the tap and waited.

Zara came home after a long night shift. The house was quiet, and Zara's stomach was empty. "What is in the fridge?" Zara asked the speaker. The speaker said there were three eggs, some cheese and half a loaf of bread. Zara could already feel a cheese sandwich coming. Then Zara said, "We're out of milk and butter. Put them on the list, because I'm going shopping on the twelfth of March." The speaker added both to the shopping list and said it would remind Zara on the morning of the twelfth. Zara ate the sandwich and went to sleep.

Hassan swept the crumbs off the desk with one hand and held a melon in the other. The melon was a gift for an aunt who was flying in that evening. "Is the flight from Cairo on time, and what gate is it at?" Hassan asked the phone. The assistant said the plane was ten minutes early and would land at gate twelve. Hassan thanked the assistant and left the office, walking past a tall glass wall where the afternoon sun was shining. The melon felt heavy, but Hassan was happy.

Person: Hi, I'm new in the city and this is my first day in the flat. Can you open the blinds and unlock the balcony door?
Assistant: I can open the blinds. I can't unlock doors, because the lock is not connected to me. Sorry about that.
Person: That's fine. Which blinds can you open?
Assistant: There are blinds in the living room and the bedroom. Which would you like?
Person: The living room first. The sum I pay for this flat is big, so I want the sun.
Assistant: The living room blinds are open now.
Person: Thanks! Open the bedroom ones later, at eight.

When you order something from a shop or online, you pick the thing, the size and how you want to get it. A lovely jacket may come in small, medium or large, and people change the size if it does not fit. Delivery can be to your home or to a shop, and some places bring things late in the evening, when the moon is already out. A cool bag keeps food cold on the way. People say, send it to my office, or I want to return this, or make it a size bigger. Most shops let you send things back within a few weeks.

A printer puts words and pictures from a computer or phone onto paper. A scanner does the opposite: it makes a picture of a paper page, like a letter or a pencil drawing, and saves it on the computer. When the printer runs low on ink, it tells you which color is gone, for example yellow. People say, print two copies, or print only page three, or scan this and send it to me. After a scan, you can scroll through the pages on the screen and check that every one looks clear. If the paper tray is empty, people ask for more paper to be added to the shopping list.

Ethan was running late, and his thumb was sore from typing all morning. He grabbed a napkin to wipe the coffee off his phone and said, "Mute alerts." The phone went quiet at once. Then he remembered his sister's post about her new puppy. He wanted to see it, but the pings would not stop coming in. "Show comments," he said. The assistant opened the post and put the newest comments on the screen. Ethan read three of them while he walked to the bus stop. Then he said, "Like it," and the assistant tapped the heart for him. He tucked the napkin in his pocket and stepped onto the bus, smiling.

Wolfgang sat at his desk, marking a stack of old letters, when his stomach growled. "I haven't eaten since breakfast," he told the speaker, "and I'm tired of my own cooking." The assistant understood. It asked if he would like to order from the noodle shop he liked last week. "Yes, the same as before," said Wolfgang. The assistant placed the order and said the food would ship from the shop in about twenty minutes. Wolfgang asked it to add a small tip for the driver. The assistant did, and read the total out loud. It was so easy that Wolfgang laughed. He went back to his letters and waited for the doorbell.

Gabriela was about to dress for her friend's party when she remembered the garden. She texted her phone: "did i water the tomatoes today". The assistant checked the sprinkler log and wrote back that the tomatoes had not been watered since yesterday morning. Gabriela typed, "ok run it for ten min, just the back bed". The assistant started the back sprinklers and set a timer. Then it asked if she wanted more water for the six pepper plants by the fence. "no they're fine," she wrote. Ten minutes later the sprinklers stopped by themselves, and the assistant sent a short message to say the job was done. Gabriela put on her blue dress and ran out the door.

A bike route is a plan for how to ride from one place to another. Most people use an app to make one. They tell it where they start and where they want to end up. Then they change it. They might ask for a shorter route, an easier route with fewer hills, or a quiet road away from cars. Some say, "Make it twenty kilometres." Others look at their most recent ride and say, "Do that one again." A club might invite everyone to a Sunday ride that ends with a pancake breakfast, and the leader shares the route with the whole group. The app then shows the distance, the speed and the next turn.

They want to hear a short summary that will describe how they slept.
- How did I sleep last night?
- Sleep report
- Describe my sleep from last night, please.
- My eyes feel full of sand, so did I sleep badly?
- Was I up a lot in the night?
- Did the automatic sleep tracking pick up my whole night?
- How did I sleep on the twelfth of March?
- When I get a free minute, could you tell me how long I slept and how many times I woke up?

Hui was holding a baby on one hip and a bag of groceries on the other when she stopped in the hall. A kite had flown over the fence into the yard, and it was getting dark. "It's so dark by the back door," she said, "and I can't see a thing out there." The assistant understood what she meant. It turned on the porch light and showed the back camera on the kitchen screen. Hui had one more question: was anyone in the yard? The assistant said the camera had seen no one for an hour. It was an easy thing to check, and she felt calmer. She put the groceries down and went to find the kite.

Picking a movie is easier when you tell the assistant what you like. Some people say, "Find me something funny." Others say, "I hate scary films, show me something calm." The assistant looks at the list of films and shows the ones that fit. You can change your mind, too. You might ask for a shorter film, an older one, or one the whole family can watch. If you want to see what is on tonight, you can ask for cinema times near you. Many people bring a kilogram of spicy popcorn, but that is up to them. When you pick one, you can ask to watch the trailer first.

Noah's dehumidifier hummed in the basement, and he sat upstairs with a cold stomach. It was almost six o'clock. "I don't care what it is," he told the phone, "I just want dinner." The assistant asked if he wanted pizza, soup or rice. "Soup," said Noah. It found a soup place that would come in about fifteen minutes. The shop had an automatic tip option, and the assistant asked if he wanted to turn it on. "Yes, but make it small," said Noah. The assistant placed the order and said the driver was on the way. Noah put out a bowl and a spoon and waited at the window.

Sunita was excited. Her grandson was playing in a concert tonight, and she wanted to find a place to park. "Find parking near the library," she said to her phone. The assistant began to look. Then Sunita remembered that her grandson would study there until the show. "No, wait," she said. "Not the library. Near the town hall." The assistant changed the search and found a lot two streets away. It said there were nineteen free spots and that the first hour cost two dollars. Sunita asked it to pay for two hours and remind her when the time was almost up. The assistant did both, and she drove off with a big smile.

They want the robot vacuum to run on a quieter, low setting.
- Go quiet.
- Use low mode.
- Vacuum more quietly, please.
- Half the noise would be nice.
- I'm on a call, turn the vacuum down.
- It's nine at night by my watch and the neighbours are asleep, so run the vacuum on low.
- Keep it low while I get dressed for the interview.
- Could you please make the vacuum quieter, because the baby is napping and I don't want to wake her?

They want to find out where they left the car.
- Where's my car?
- Where did I park?
- I only remember that I parked near a tree, where is the car?
- I cast my eyes over the whole lot and can't find my car.
- The rain is like a curtain and I can't see the car, so where is it?
- Show me where I left the car on the map.
- Which level did I park on?
- Excuse me, I came out of the late film, it is dark, and I cannot remember where I left my car, so could you please tell me where it is?

They want a timer for a short break.
- 10 min break timer
- start a break timr for ten minutes
- timer for a break, 15 minutes
- i need to leave my desk for a bit, set a 5 min timer
- set a timer for the last break of the day
- im going to refill my liter bottle, remind me in 10 minutes to come back
- tell me when my break is over
- Could you please set a ten minute timer so I can rest my eyes and then get back to work?

Hyun had just finished a night shift and her eyes were closing. She was walking home when she remembered her pants were still at the tailor. "Remind me to pick up my pants," she told her phone, "when I'm near the town square." The assistant said it would. Then Hyun said, "Not tomorrow morning, though, I'll be asleep. And don't remind me at home, please." The assistant understood. It set the reminder for the square only and said it would not ring tomorrow morning. Hyun yawned, thanked it, and went to bed. In the afternoon her phone buzzed as she crossed the square, and she walked into the shop.

name: morning_headlines
does: Reads out the top news of the day, so you can wipe the counter or fill a bottle while you listen.
inputs: a topic such as sport or local news; how many headlines you want; optional: a time to read them every day
people say:
- What's going on in the world today?
- Read me the news.
- Anything big happen overnight?
- Give me three headlines about my town.
- Tell me the sports news every morning at seven.
- I have two minutes, what should I know?

They want to know what a price abroad is in their own money, so there is no dangerous surprise at the till.
- How much is that in euros?
- What's the rate today?
- What is five hundred zloty in dollars?
- I'm selling hay from my field to a buyer in Poland, what is that price in my money?
- It will hurt if this costs double what I think, so what is it in pounds?
- Is the price in yen more or less than eighty dollars?
- Half of this bill is in Swiss francs, what is the whole thing in euros?
- Could you please tell me what a hundred pounds is worth in Japanese yen right now?

Food delivery lets you order a meal from a shop and have it brought to your door. You pick the food, check the price and say where to bring it. Then people change things. They ask for the food to come sooner, or they ask what time it will arrive. Some say, "Be careful with the soup, it spills." Many add a tip for the driver. If my uncle orders pizza for the whole family, he says, "Add a tip, but not too big." When the driver is close, the app tells you. If you still owe money for the order, it asks you to pay before the food comes.

Measuring things means using a number and a unit, like grams, metres or degrees. People use units every day. In the bathroom you might step on a scale to see your weight. In the kitchen you pour water into a shallow bowl and check how many cups it holds. When you ask a smart speaker, "How many cups is a litre?", it changes one unit into another for you. If the speaker is quiet, say "unmute" first so you can hear the answer. People also say, "Make it in inches," or "Give me that in Celsius." That just means they want the same amount shown in a different unit.

A kettle boils water so you can make tea fast. On a sunny morning, you might fill it and press a button, and the dog waits by your feet for a bit of toast. People change how these machines work all the time. They say, "Heat it to eighty degrees," or "Keep it warm for ten minutes." With an oven, they might say, "Preheat to two hundred," or "Cut the time by half." A coffee machine can cast a nice smell through the kitchen when it starts. A dishwasher is told, "Run the short wash," or "Start it after dinner." The words are plain, and the machine does the rest.

A podcast is a show you can listen to whenever you like. An audiobook is a book that someone reads out loud. Both remember where you stopped, so you can close the app and come back later to the same place. My goal is to finish one book each month, but I can't wait for the next episode of my favourite show. People change a few things when they listen. They say, "Play it faster," "Skip forward thirty seconds," or "Go back to the start of the chapter." They also say, "Where did I leave off?" and the app tells them. It is a simple way to enjoy a story while you walk or cook.

Niamh knelt in the garden with one foot on the spade. She was writing a note about healthy soil for the village newsletter, and she was using her phone. "How many words have I got?" she asked. The assistant counted and said there were two hundred and ten. "The newsletter only wants one hundred and fifty," said Niamh. "Tell me which six sentences are the longest." The assistant read them out. Niamh cut two of them. Then she said, "Raise the text size, my eyes are tired." The assistant made the letters bigger. She read the note one more time, and the count was just right. She hit send and went back to her roses.

Adebayo woke up at three in the morning and could not get back to sleep. The cat had hidden under the table, and the bedside light was too bright. "Make the light half as bright," he said to the speaker. The assistant dimmed it. Then Adebayo said, "And my alarm is far too loud. Make it half as loud tomorrow." The assistant lowered the alarm volume and said it was set for seven. Adebayo thanked it, closed his eyes, and listened to the quiet room. A few minutes later he was asleep, with the cat curled up on the blanket.

Person: Can you book me a taxi for tomorrow morning?
Assistant: Yes. Where should it pick you up?
Person: At my house. And save that address for next time.
Assistant: I will. How many people are going? There will be four of you if it is your family, so I need to know the right car size.
Person: Just three, me and my two friends.
Assistant: Good. What time do you need the car?
Person: Nine o'clock. Please make a note that we have small bags.
Assistant: I made a note for the driver. Please remember that there is a minimum fare for this trip. Shall I book it for nine?
Person: Yes, please.

Seo-yeon came home after a long night shift. The street was dark, and her building had no lights up for the holiday. She was tired, but her kids would wake soon. "Hang lights," she said to her phone. The assistant said it could not hang them, but it could turn on the lights she had already put up on the porch. It did. Then she said, "Play carols." The assistant played a quiet song through the home network. She asked it to keep the volume at the minimum, so the kids could sleep a little longer. She smelled the fry pan from the neighbours' kitchen and smiled. Then she lay down for a short rest.

They want the daily news on the radio.
- put on the news
- radio news pls
- play the daily news on the radio
- whats on the radio news right now
- tune to the news station
- my friends are comming for tea at four, put the daily news on while i set the table
- turn on the radio and find the news
- Could you please switch on the radio news, because I would like to hear what happened today before I invite anyone over?

Energy at home means the electricity, heat and light a house uses. People want to use less of it, because it costs money. A solar panel on the roof makes power from the sun, but on a day with a pale winter sky it makes less. Most apps show you how much you use. After the kids finish their homework and go to bed, you may want the lights and screens off. People say, "Turn everything off downstairs," "Lower the heat by two degrees," or "Cancel the heating for tonight." They also ask, "How much power did we use today?" Small changes like these add up on the bill.

name: school_run_planner
does: Plans the morning trip to school, so the kids can walk, ride the bus or get a lift, and arrive in a comfortable amount of time.
inputs: the child's name; the school; the time school starts; how you want to travel
people say:
- How do I get Mia to school by eight?
- When does the school bus come?
- Plan the school run for tomorrow.
- Will we make it if we leave at quarter past?
- Remind me when it's time to go.
- I want the kids to walk today, how long will it take?

Radio is a way to hear music, news and talk without choosing each song. A waiter in a small cafe might leave a station playing all day. You pick a station by its name or its number on the dial. People say, "Put on the news," or "Find some calm music." If it is too loud, they say, "Turn it down," or "Make it a whisper." Some people want a different station and say, "Change the channel," or "Find the sports one." A smart radio can also remember your favourite station and play it when you say, "Play my usual." It is the same radio, but now you ask for what you want.

Aoife was in the kitchen with the baby on her arm when her meeting was about to start. Her laptop battery was only half full, so she asked the assistant, "Can you tell me how much battery I have?" It said fifty percent. "That's not enough for an hour," she said. "Set a reminder for ten minutes before, so I plug it in." The assistant did. Then she said, "Join the call at ten and use a plain white background, please." At ten the assistant joined the meeting, and the screen looked clean and simple. Aoife smiled, put the baby in the chair and sat down to talk.

Moussa was a cook, and the kitchen had been very hot all day. At night he wanted a short workout. "Give me a workout," he said to his phone, "three sets of ten push-ups." The assistant began to set it up. Then Moussa thought about his sore back. "Actually, make it twelve push-ups, no, wait, ten, I'm not a person who should push too hard today." The assistant changed the plan to three sets of ten. It said that lifting heavy things with a bad back can be dangerous, so it left out the weights. Moussa laughed, ate a slice of bread, and started his first set.

They want the pool water to be warmer.
- Warm it up.
- Make the pool a bit warmer.
- Two degrees warmer, please.
- The water is flat-out freezing, heat it up.
- The pool behind the hedge is far too cold for the kids.
- We just bought this pool, so please heat it to thirty degrees.
- Raise the temperature by half a degree every hour until it feels right.
- Could you please turn the heater up, because my friends are coming to swim this afternoon and I would like the water to be nice and warm?

Camila did not know much about phones, and tonight she was nervous. She had to travel in the morning for a holiday with her cousins, and the room felt chilly. She picked up her phone and typed quickly: "set alram for 5 am". The assistant understood her message, even with the small mistake. It set the alarm and said, "Your alarm is set for five in the morning." Camila typed, "thank u, and turn off the lite". The assistant turned off the bedroom light. She pulled the blanket up to her chin and fell asleep thinking about the beach.

A car alarm is a loud sound that warns you when someone touches the car. Most cars also have other warnings. A light on the dash comes on when the tyres are low or when the fuel is almost gone. People who drive a lot like to check these things before a trip. They say, "How much fuel do I have?" or "Are my tyres okay?" On a cold day they say, "Warm up the car." After a long drive they say, "Where did I park?" Friends who share a car might split the cost of fuel. If something goes wrong, a local garage can help. The words are simple, and the car tells you what it needs.

Beatriz owned a small bakery, and the best cookies sold out by noon. Tonight she was excited, because a big order was due in the morning, and she was working late. She wanted to know the shop was safe. She typed to the assistant: "turn on the cmeras and arm the alarm". It understood her message in spite of the typo. The assistant switched on both cameras and set the alarm. It also said the back door was open. Beatriz ran to shut it, then asked the assistant to tell her if anyone arrived. It said it would send her a message. She locked the front door and went home.

Rodrigo was a busy parent, and the only free time he had was after the kids went to bed. "Give me a workout," he said, "medium hard, about twenty minutes." The assistant made a plan with squats, push-ups and a plank. "Double the squats," said Rodrigo, "but half the plank." The assistant changed it. Rodrigo started, and the children's lullaby kept playing in his mind. He could hear his daughter sing from her room, and her voice made him smile. He did not want her to see him sweat. When his mouth was dry, he asked for a short rest. The assistant counted down ninety seconds, then told him to start the next set.

Emi drove a taxi, and on Friday night she had a long week behind her. She was waiting in the car with the heater on, to keep her hands warm. A customer wanted a ride from the station, and she asked the assistant to pick the best pickup spot. "Don't send me to the front of the station," she said, "the buses block it. And don't pick a spot with a high step, my passenger is in a wheelchair." The assistant looked at the map and chose a flat spot on the side street. It said she would arrive in six minutes. Emi thanked it, put the car in gear and drove.

Accessibility means making a phone or a computer easy for everyone to use. Some people cannot see the screen well, so they ask the phone to read text out loud. Others tap the screen with a finger and find the words too small. They say, "Make the text bigger," or "Read this page to me." People who find bright screens hard say, "Dim the screen." Voice control is for people who cannot touch the phone at all. They say, "Open my messages," or "Go back." If the phone does something wrong, they say, "No, not that one," and it tries again. The goal is to let the person decide how to use it.

Podcasts and audiobooks are made to be heard, not read. You can listen while you cook, walk or drive. The app keeps your place, so if you stop half way through an episode, it begins again in the same spot. People use it in a few ways. In the summer they listen on long walks and say, "Play the next episode," or "Go back one minute." Some say, "Play it at one and a half speed." Others want help to wake up and say, "Wake me at seven with my show." When a chapter ends, they say, "Start the next one," and the story goes on.

They want to see their newest notes first.
- Show my newest notes.
- Latest notes first, please.
- Put my notes in order, newest on top.
- Read me the last two notes.
- My mouse is broken, so can you open my notes by voice?
- Show me half of the list, only the recent ones.
- Give me a nice short list of what I wrote this week.
- Could you please open my notes and put the most recent ones in order at the top?

Person: Count the words and fix the spelling, please.
Assistant: Sure. Which file do you want me to use?
Person: The one from this morning. I'm in a hurry, my pages just fell on the floor and I need the soft copy.
Assistant: I see two files from this morning. One is called Report and one is called Letter. Which one?
Person: The report.
Assistant: The report has nine hundred and forty words. I fixed three spelling mistakes. Do you want me to print it too?
Person: Can you? My printer is in another room.
Assistant: I am sorry, I cannot print from here. I can send the file to your email.

Aroha was out in the garden pulling weeds, and the day was cold. She knew she would work for hours if no one stopped her, so she called out to her phone, "Quiet hour." The assistant understood. It turned off her notifications for sixty minutes. A little later, she spoke again. "Move break." The assistant asked if she meant to move her break to later. "Yes," said Aroha. The assistant changed the break from three o'clock to four and said it would ring when the time came. Aroha went back to her weeds, with her hands warm in her gloves.

In an emergency, the first job is to be safe, and then to get help. A smoke alarm makes a loud sound when it senses smoke. If it goes silent, the battery may be dead, so people say, "Remind me to change the battery." During a power cut, a phone can light the room and call for help. People say, "Call the emergency number," or "Tell my sister where I am." If a street is flooded, they may need to drive another way and say, "Find a road that is not flooded." Even a leaf stuck in a drain can block water, so some ask the assistant to warn them when it rains hard.

Silvia was lying on her bed, feeling calm, when a package arrived. Inside was a tiny plant for her desk. She wanted to show her friends how it would grow, so she grabbed her phone and typed: "take a pic of my plnt". The assistant opened the camera and took the photo. Then Silvia typed, "put it in the plants album and send to maya". The assistant saved the photo in the album and sent a copy to Maya. A minute later Maya answered with a row of hearts. Silvia put the plant on the window sill and set a reminder to take another picture next week.

Bo did not like new phones, but his daughter had set one up for him. On Saturday he needed to go to the market. He held the phone close and said, "Book me a taxi and show me when it comes." The assistant asked where to pick him up. "At the front of my building," Bo said. The assistant booked the ride and put a small map on the screen. It showed the car getting closer. When the taxi was two streets away, it said, "Your car will arrive in two minutes." Bo took his keys, remembered to lock the door, and walked out to wait.

Privacy means deciding who can see your things, and a password is the key that keeps others out. A good password is long and hard to guess. Names like lemon123 are easy for others to guess, so people change them. They say, "Change my password," or "Make me a strong one." A phone can also lock itself after a minute, and people say, "Lock my phone after thirty seconds." Some prefer a face or a fingerprint instead of a code. On a humid day your fingers may be damp, and the print may not work, so a code is handy. People also ask, "Who can see my photos?" and change it to just family.

Tamar sat by the window and watched grey clouds roll over the school across the road. Her grandchildren would walk home in an hour. "Will it rain this afternoon?" she asked the speaker. The assistant said yes, it would start at three. "How hard?" asked Tamar. The assistant said it would be heavy for about a dozen minutes and then turn to light rain. Tamar wanted the children to stay healthy, so she asked, "Tell me what they should wear." The assistant said raincoats and boots. Tamar asked it to run the dryer, then sent a short message to the children: bring your hoods.

Lakshmi came home after a night shift and wanted to relax with her knitting book. She said to her assistant, "I know it is early, and I am tired, but could you please schedule a short reminder at four o'clock to read the next chapter of my knitting book? I would like to sleep first, and I do not want to lose my place." The assistant said it would. It set the reminder and asked if she wanted a quiet sound. "Yes, please," said Lakshmi. She pulled the curtains and fell asleep. At four the soft chime woke her, and she picked up her needles.

Ming had just woken up, and his stomach was already empty. He rubbed his eyes and said to the speaker, "Order me a bagel and tell me when it's close." The assistant asked which shop. "The one on the corner," said Ming. It placed the order and said the delivery would take about fifteen minutes. Ming went to the kitchen and filled the water tank of his coffee machine. He burned the toast he had started earlier, so he threw it out. Soon the speaker said, "Your bagel is close." Ming opened the door and the driver handed him a warm bag.

Baking turns flour, water and yeast into bread. The dough has to rest and rise before it goes in the oven. People often change the time, because it depends on the room. On a cold day the dough takes longer. They say, "Set a timer for one hour," or "Tell me when it has doubled." A cake goes straight into the oven after mixing, and people say, "Preheat to one hundred and eighty." Some like to boil water first for a steamy oven. When a second tray is ready, they say, "Add ten minutes." The oven beeps when the baking is done, and the assistant can say it again.

name: parcel_watcher
does: Tells you when a parcel is near your home, so you can be there on the weekend to sign for it, and it keeps a note of the bottom shelf of the mailbox where small ones go.
inputs: the tracking number or shop name; the day you want it; whether you need to sign
people say:
- Where's my package?
- Has my parcel come yet?
- Tell me when the mail truck is near.
- Will someone be there to sign for it on Saturday?
- Did the postman leave anything in my mailbox?
- Can they bring it next week instead, I won't be home?

A smart speaker is a small device that listens to your voice and does things for you. You can ask it for music, the weather or a timer. People change how it works with simple words. They say, "Turn it up," or "Lower the volume." A heavy sound in the bass might be too much, so they say, "Less bass." You can put a speaker in each room and say, "Play the music everywhere." To keep the sound in one place, they say, "Disconnect the kitchen speaker." Some speakers let each person set up their own voice, so the device knows who is talking. If you stand a foot away, it hears you well.

On Wednesday afternoon, Hassan was in the office kitchen when a coworker burned her hand on the kettle. Hassan grabbed his phone. "Hey assistant, how long should I run cold water on a burn?" he asked. The assistant said to hold the burn under cool running water for at least ten minutes, and not to use ice. Hassan helped her to the sink.
Then he said, "Read me the steps for a small burn." The assistant read them slowly: cool the burn, cover it with a clean, loose bandage, and do not pop any blisters. The first aid box on the wall was almost empty, so Hassan said, "Put bandages on my shopping list." The assistant put them on the list.
After a while his coworker felt well again. Hassan remembered that the company had spent two thousand dollars on safety training last year, but the box still needed a refill. He asked the assistant to remind him on Friday to buy more supplies.

Person: Can you tell me when the water bill is due and remind me two days before?
Assistant: Sure. Which water company is it with?
Person: The city one. I forget the brand of the meter, but the bill comes from the city.
Assistant: Got it. The city water bill is due on the twentieth. I will remind you on the eighteenth.
Person: Great. Can you also pay my rent from my savings?
Assistant: I am sorry, I can't make payments. I can point you to the rent due date and remind you to pay it yourself.
Person: Okay, please remind me. I want a quiet evening without worrying.
Assistant: Done. I will remind you on the first at six in the evening.

Tariq was peeling oranges for the kids when the kitchen got too loud. The twins were shouting about a cartoon, and the baby was crying. He had no free hand, so he spoke to the speaker on the shelf. "Play something calm, and turn it down a bit," he said.
The speaker started a soft piano playlist and lowered the volume. Tariq smiled. "Skip this one, it sounds sad," he added a minute later, and the speaker jumped to the next song.
The kids slowed down and listened. After a stretch of quiet, the oldest girl asked for something with drums. "Play a dozen songs with drums," Tariq said. The speaker made a short playlist of twelve songs and began the first one. Tariq finished the oranges and put them on the table, and the whole family ate in a good mood.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a name, a number, and sometimes an address or a birthday. It helps you call or write to people without remembering every number. Often you need to change a card. A friend moves, so you say, "Update Lena's address." A sister gets a new phone, so you say, "Change Dad's number to this one." If a strange number calls and you want to keep it, you say, "Save this number as the plumber." Some people keep numbers on paper inside a backpack, but a saved contact is easier to find. You can also say, "Delete the old number for Sam" or "Fix the spelling of Maria's name." With a saved card, nobody has to cry over a lost number.

People want to change how many servings a recipe makes, even on a busy night when the scale's charger is dead.
Halve it
Make this for two
Can you trim this recipe in half?
I only need six portions, not twelve
Double everything, we have guests
How much flour do I need for three people instead of eight?
Turn the pancake recipe into one for four servings
Could you please scale the soup recipe up to ten servings for me, because my cousins are coming over?

Rizal sat on the porch with a cup of tea and a calendar full of circles. He was a retired teacher, and he liked to count things. "Assistant, how many days until my granddaughter's birthday on the fourth of July?" he asked.
The assistant counted and said there were thirty-one days left. Rizal nodded. "And how old will she be?" The assistant said she would turn nine.
He felt a free afternoon stretching out in front of him, so he asked one more thing. "Tell me how many days are in the school holiday, from June first to August twelfth." The assistant did the sums and answered with seventy-three days.
Rizal wrote the number on the back of a jar label and stuck it to the fridge. Then he put the dishes in the sink to wash, humming, and went to look for a gift.

Kasia was making dinner for forty guests at the restaurant, and the butter had not come. She stirred the pot and looked at the clock. "I'm running out of butter, and nothing has arrived yet," she said to her phone.
The assistant understood that she wanted to know about her order. It opened her last order and said the box of butter was still on the truck, with six stops to go. A little meter on the screen showed the delivery was about half done.
Kasia felt sad for a moment. "Can you tell the driver to hurry?" she asked. The assistant said it could not do that, but it could send her a message the moment the truck was close. Kasia agreed. She used the last bit of butter on the first pan and waited, and twenty minutes later her phone buzzed that the truck was outside.

name: tune_drink
does: Makes a drink stronger, weaker, sweeter or less sweet, and starts the machine to run a fresh cup after a short nap in the morning.
inputs: which drink it is, and whether to make it stronger, weaker, sweeter or less sweet
people say:
- Make my coffee stronger
- Less sugar in my tea, please
- This smoothie is too sweet
- I barely slept, I need something with more kick
- Can you make it a bit milder?
- Same as yesterday, but sweeter

Giulia sat on her bed with her phone, looking at a pair of pants in an online shop from London. The price said fifty pounds. She texted the assistant. "how much is 50 pounds in euros? i don't want a long answer, just the number"
The assistant answered with one short line: about fifty-eight euros. Giulia frowned. "is there a nearby shop that sells the same pants? not online, i don't want to wait for shipping"
The assistant looked and found a store ten minutes away by bus. It showed the opening hours and said it closed at eight. Giulia sat up. "ok save that store to my places and remind me to go tomorrow after school," she wrote. The assistant saved the store and set the reminder for four o'clock the next day. Giulia put the phone down, happy that she did not have to pay for shipping.

A parent wants screens to end at a set time, so the kids can go outside or sit by the fireplace while dinner gets a stir.
Turn off the tablets at five
Screen time is over before lunch on Sunday
Stop the TV for the kids at half past six tonight
Can you shut down the game console after supper on Friday?
Lock the kids' tablets until tomorrow morning
I want the screens off by the time the soup is ready on Saturday
Please switch off the children's devices at seven every school night so they have time to play and get ready for bed
Tell the kids it's time to stop, and cut the wifi in their rooms before lunch on Sunday

Ananya, a retired teacher, sat at the kitchen table with her square tin of tea leaves. She had won a small prize at the village fair for her ginger tea, and she wanted to make it again. She typed quickly on her tablet: "make my tea strnger and save it as my usual"
The assistant understood her typing. It told her it had made the next cup stronger by a little, then saved the new setting under the name "my usual." Ananya smiled and pressed the button on the kettle.
"Can you also make it less sweet next time?" she asked out loud. The assistant said it would lower the sugar by one spoon from now on. When the tea was ready, it was just right, and Ananya poured it into her best cup and sat by the window to enjoy it.

name: park_time_left
does: Tells you how many minutes are left on your parking and how many dollars it costs to extend it, so a strange street never leads to a ticket.
inputs: the car plate or spot number, and the street or lot name
people say:
- How long do I have left?
- Am I about to get a ticket?
- Keep my parking going for another hour
- I don't want to cry over a fine, check my time
- What do I owe for this spot?
- Tell me when it's about to run out

Marlene sat down with her breakfast and a mug of tea. She was not good with technology, and the little smart speaker on the table still confused her. But she wanted to hear her book. In a gentle voice she said, "Read book."
The speaker answered, "Do you want to continue your audiobook, The Garden Letters?" Marlene said yes. The speaker found the place where she stopped the night before and started playing from chapter six.
A few minutes later the narrator spoke too fast. "Slower," said Marlene. The speaker lowered the speed a little. When the doorbell rang, she said, "Pause." The speaker stopped at once. After she talked with the neighbor, she said, "Come back," and the story went on from the same sentence. Marlene was pleased, and she finished her toast while the story continued.

Giulia worked as a cook in a small cafe, and her days were long. On Sunday she remembered that her sister's birthday was in November, and she felt a push of worry. She did not want to forget again.
"Remind me to buy a present for my sister next Tuesday at noon," she said to her phone. The assistant set the reminder and said it would remind her at twelve o'clock.
"Also, what could I get her? She likes plants and tea," Giulia asked. The assistant listed a few ideas: a small herb pot, a box of mint tea, or a pretty cup. Giulia liked the pot and the tea together.
"Put those two on my list," she said. The assistant did. Giulia felt happy and went back to chopping onions, sure that this year the gift would come on time.

Person: put on the cookin show
Assistant: Sure. Which channel is it on?
Person: i dont remember. its the one with the lady who makes cream cakes
Assistant: I can scan the guide for cooking shows. I found one called Sweet Hands on channel twelve. Is that the one?
Person: yes thats it. and turn on the subtitels
Assistant: Done. The subtitles are on. Do you want me to record the next episode too?
Person: yes please. last time i missed it and the cake was stale by the time i saw the recipe
Assistant: I will record it every Thursday at seven.

A work meeting is a time when people join one call to talk, share their screens, and follow an agenda. The agenda is a short list of what will be discussed, and it keeps things from running long. People often ask to change a meeting. If a morning meeting is too early, someone says, "Move it to ten." If a colleague is late, they say, "Push it back by fifteen minutes." If you need to rush to join, you can say, "Join my next call." During the call, people say, "Share my screen" or "Mute me." A false start can happen when the link is wrong, so people also ask, "Send me the right link again."

Darius stood outside the clinic with his keys in his hand and a sour feeling in his stomach. He was late for the dentist and had parked in a hurry. He had only ten minutes left on his ticket, and he had just eaten a boiled egg that tasted bad.
"I only have ten minutes on my parking, and my appointment is an hour long," he told his phone.
The assistant understood that he needed more time. It opened the parking app, found his spot on Elm Street, and asked, "Do you want to extend it by one hour?" Darius said yes. The assistant paid for the extra time and showed the new end time on the screen. Then it set a reminder ten minutes before the end. Darius could point his thoughts at his teeth and nothing else.

In a cold town, people who prefer a warm house, and wear a sour face on frosty mornings, ask for the heating to go up.
Warmer, please
Set it to seventy
It's freezing in here
Turn the thermostat up a little
Make the living room warmer before I wake up
Can you get the house to seventy-two by six this evening?
The bedroom is cold, can you heat it for half an hour?

Adam did not like gadgets, but his daughter had set up a speaker in the living room and told him to try it. He stood on the lovely wool rug in his socks and spoke loudly. "Start my morning workout and keep time for me."
The speaker said, "Starting a ten minute workout. Ready?" Adam said yes. It counted twenty squats and then ten push-ups, and Adam huffed. In the middle he got tired. "Slow down and give me a rest," he said. The speaker gave him thirty seconds to breathe.
At the end, Adam asked how many days of rest he should take before the next workout. The speaker said one day was a good idea. It also asked if it should keep a record of the workout. "Yes, please," said Adam. Down by the river, his daughter later saw his smile on a photo.

Anh was in the garden planting beans when a sharp pain shot through her tooth. She felt it every time she bit down. She wiped her hands on her apron and took out her phone.
"Book dentist," she said.
The assistant asked, "Which dentist? Do you want Dr. Park, whom you saw last year?" Anh nodded. "Yes, Dr. Park. Soonest," she said.
The assistant looked at the calendar and found a free spot on Thursday at ten. It was at the clinic on the west side of town. "Shall I book that?" it asked. Anh said, "Yes." The assistant booked it and put a note in her calendar. Then it asked if she wanted a reminder the night before. Anh said yes, and went back to her beans, feeling better already.

Zeynep sat at her desk and heard a sound from her phone. A stranger had tried to connect to her bluetooth speaker again. She worried about her privacy. It was a bad habit of the neighbor's laptop, but she did not want anyone to see her photos.
"Block every new device that tries to connect to my phone," she told the assistant. The assistant turned on a setting so that only the devices she had approved could connect. It showed her three old devices on the list and asked which ones to remove.
"Remove the two I don't use," said Zeynep. The assistant removed them. Then she asked it to lock her phone with a longer passcode, double the length of the old one. The assistant guided her through the new passcode, and Zeynep felt safer.

Tala woke up to a loud noise outside her window. She rubbed her eyes and heard a truck on the highway nearby. She was waiting for a package, and today was supposed to be the day. She still lay in bed with the blanket up to her chin.
"I think the truck is outside, but I don't hear anyone at the door," she said to her phone.
The assistant guessed that she wanted to know about the delivery. It checked her order and said the package was out for delivery, due between nine and noon. It was now the middle of the morning. The driver had tried to shout up to her flat, the note said, but nobody had answered.
Tala jumped up. "Ask them to come back," she said. The assistant sent a message asking the driver to try again, and Tala hurried to the door in her socks.

Rosa came home after a long night shift at the hospital. Her eyes were heavy, but she remembered the electricity bill. She stood in the hallway, holding her mop, and talked to her phone.
"Remind me to pay the electric bill every Monday at nine until I tell you to stop," she said.
The assistant said, "Every Monday at nine, starting this Monday. Is that right?" Rosa said yes. Then she frowned. "I think there's an old reminder about the water bill that I don't need now. Delete it." The assistant found it and deleted it.
"Do you want to see your bills with special due dates this month?" it asked. Rosa nodded. The assistant read out two bills: the electric bill, due on the fifteenth, and the phone bill, due on the twenty-second. Rosa thanked it, put away the mop, and finally went to bed.

A grocery list is a short list of things you need to buy. It saves you from forgetting milk or eggs and from buying too much. People keep it in a phone, on the fridge, or in a notebook. When you run out of something, you say, "Put eggs on the list." When you buy it, you say, "Take eggs off." If the list gets mixed up, you can say, "Restart the list" and start fresh. At the least, a good list says what you need and how much. Before the weekend people also ask, "What is in the fridge?" or "What do we need for dinner?" On a trip to the sea, they say, "Make a list for a picnic."

Compare my bills

I would be grateful if you could line up this year's heating bills with last year's, since I'm trying to decide whether to move to a smaller place.

Baking turns flour, water, yeast and sugar into bread, cakes and cookies. Each recipe has a time for the dough to rest and rise, and a time for the oven. People often change the plan. If a cake looks too brown, they say, "Dim the oven" or "Lower the heat to a hundred and fifty." If the dough is slow, they ask, "Add ten more minutes to the timer." Many bakers buy flour from a local mill and mix it in a blender or with their hands. When the cookies are ready, they say, "Stop the timer," or "How long until the bread is done?" The words are simple, but they help the oven and the baker work together.

A phone is a small computer that you carry. It has a battery, a bright screen and room for photos and apps. People change a few settings every day. If the screen hurts their eyes, they say, "Make the screen dimmer." If they are in a meeting, they say, "Turn on do not disturb." When the phone is almost full, they ask, "How much storage is left?" and "Delete my old photos." If a guest wants to use the wifi, they say, "Show me the wifi password." People also ask the phone to search for things, like "Search for a pizza place nearby." When the battery is low, they say, "Turn on battery saver," so an old phone can last all day.

Roya was not good with technology, but she knew she needed a new password. Her grandson had told her that a good password was long and not easy to guess. She sat in her blue armchair and looked at the tablet.
"Excuse me, assistant, would you please help me change my email password? A man phoned me from the mall yesterday and asked many questions, and now I'm worried," she said politely.
The assistant said it was glad to help. It asked her to name a new password that she would remember, and it explained that she should not use a birthday. Roya chose a line from her favorite song. The assistant checked that it was strong enough and saved it in the password list. It also told her never to give the password to anyone on the phone. Roya felt much better.

An emergency is when something goes wrong fast, like smoke in the kitchen, a power cut, or water on the floor. Homes have a few simple helpers. A smoke alarm makes a loud sound when it senses smoke. A flashlight helps in a power cut. Many families keep a plain list of numbers on the fridge. People can also ask a phone for help. They say, "Call for help," "Call my mother," or "Where is the nearest hospital?" After a flood, they might say, "Turn off the water." It is good to practice before a real emergency. A bucket of water might weigh many pounds, and a gallon of water weighs about eight, so people should move slowly and ask for help.

Francesca, a grandmother, took her pills every morning, but lately she forgot the second one in the evening. Her granddaughter had put a smart display on the kitchen counter, and Francesca decided to try it.
"Remind me to take my blue pill every evening at eight," she said.
The display answered, "I will remind you every evening at eight. Do you want the reminder to be louder than your alarm?" Francesca said, "A little louder, yes." The display made the sound a bit louder.
Then she remembered her car. "Also remind me weekly to check the tire air. And if I say later, wait half an hour," she said. The display agreed. It would remind her every Saturday morning about the tire. Francesca felt proud. Now she did not have to lower her head in shame at the doctor's when she forgot.

Rizal woke up late, with his hair in all directions and his mouth dry. The fan above the bed was still turning. He remembered, with a jolt, that his car was parked on a street with a two hour limit, and it had been three. He took the phone from the table, and he did not want to wash his face yet.
"Excuse me, assistant, could you please tell me how much time I have left on my parking? I fell asleep and I'm afraid I got a ticket. I need to know the true situation before I go outside," he said.
The assistant checked and said the parking had run out forty minutes ago, but no ticket had been marked yet. It offered to pay for another hour. Rizal said yes, thanked it, and ran out to move his car.

A to-do list is a list of tasks you want to finish. It helps you remember them and see what is left. Some people keep it on paper, and others in a phone. Each task can have a priority, which means how important it is. A healthy habit is to check things off when they are done. People often change their lists with short words. They say, "Put call the dentist on my list," "Move laundry to tomorrow," or "Mark the report as done." At the end of the week, someone might say, "Empty the list" to remove old tasks. They might also ask, "What is on my list today?" or "What is the most important thing?" Even a microwave reminder, like heating lunch, can go on the list.

A daily medicine is a pill or drop that someone takes once a day, often at the same time. A dose is the amount to take. Doctors tell people how much and when, and the label on the box repeats it. People use their phone to help with this. They say, "Remind me to take my pill at eight," or "Change the reminder to nine." If a symptom comes back, they might ask, "Book a visit with my doctor." Sometimes a pill is too hard to swallow, and someone asks, "Can I pull the tablet in half?" That is a question for the doctor or the pharmacy, because the answer is on the page of the leaflet. A phone should never decide on a dose alone.

Ayesha was a busy mother of three, and on Saturday she wanted to take her son on a bike ride before the rain came. She put her phone in her pocket and rolled the bike out of the garage, under the roof of the shed.
"Find me a bike route to the lake. I don't want hills, and I don't want busy roads," she said.
The assistant thought for a second. It found a flat path along the river, six miles long, with a quiet park at the end. "This route is mostly north of the town," it said. "Shall I start the directions?"
"Yes, and tell me how far we have gone every two miles," said Ayesha. The assistant started and called out the distance, and her son rang his bell at each one.

Learning a language is a bit like learning to ride a bike. You start slowly and practice often. Many people take a lesson once a week and use their phones to help in between. They say, "How do you say good morning in Spanish?" or "Translate this sign for me." If a word is hard, they ask, "How do you spell it?" or "Say it again, slower." Travelers may say, "Teach me five useful phrases." Before they buy a ticket in another country, they like to know a few words. A thin phrase book can fit in a pocket, but a phone is faster. When they have learned a phrase, they say, "Save it to my list," so they can practice it later.

Lei was a student with a tight budget and a big appetite. On Friday night, she wanted to eat out with friends, but she did not want to go to a place that cost too much. She picked up her phone on the public bus.
"Find a noodle place nearby that is cheaper than the last one we went to," she said.
The assistant showed three places. It said the second one was half the price of the last restaurant, and it had a farm theme with a painting of a cow on the wall. "Do you want to book a table?" it asked. Lei said yes, for four people at seven.
"Heat the leftovers at home first, so I don't come hungry," joked Lei. The assistant said it could not heat food, but it booked the table. Lei grinned and got off the bus.

Bjorn woke up on the sofa with a stiff neck. The room was gray, and on the screen of his phone a podcast was still paused. He had fallen asleep while listening, and he could not remember where he stopped.
"Where did I fall asleep?" he mumbled.
The assistant said he had been listening to a history podcast about old bridges, and he stopped at minute thirty-one of episode nine. It asked if he wanted to find the last part he remembered. Bjorn said, "Go back four minutes." The assistant went back and played from there.
He listened while he made coffee. When the host talked about a meter-long stone, he laughed. "Play the next four episodes in a row," he said. The assistant lined up the next four, and Bjorn stretched his arms and drank his coffee.

Television shows you channels, movies and streaming programs, and you control it with a remote. Most people use a few simple words to ask for things. They say, "Turn on the news," "Change to channel five," or "Louder, please." If a show is hard to follow, they ask for subtitles. Before a holiday, a family might say, "Record the holiday movie for Saturday night." When the list of saved shows gets long, they say, "Remove the old shows." Someone who is polite may even say, "Could you please pause it for a minute?" The remote has buttons for all of this, but many people now find it easier to simply talk.

An air conditioner cools a room by pulling in warm air, taking the heat out of it, and blowing cool air back. People use it to stay comfortable on hot days. The most common change is the temperature. A person might say, make it cooler, set it to twenty-two degrees, or it's too cold in here, turn it down. Some people divide the house into zones, so the bedroom stays cool while the kitchen does not. A fan is simpler: it only moves air, which feels cooler on the skin. People say, make the fan faster, slow it down, or turn it off at midnight. A pale curtain keeps the sun out, and even a potato stays fresh longer in a cool kitchen.

A smart lock lets people open the front door without a key. It is for letting family in, keeping strangers out, and knowing the door is shut. People change a few things about it. They ask it to lock the door at night, to unlock it for a friend, or to show who is at the door. A polite visitor rings the bell, and the camera shows their face on the phone. If you wish to check the door from work, you might say, is the front door locked? or lock up the house. For a garage door you say, open the garage, or close the garage. If a lock breaks, the shop may give a refund, and the new lock works with the same words.

Paolo was in the middle of making dinner when he found a greasy pizza box and a jar with a little sauce left in it. His hands were messy, so he spoke to the kitchen speaker. "Excuse me, could you please explain which bin the pizza box goes in? I have to take the rubbish out before the truck comes, and last week I put the wrong things in and got a note on my bin."
The speaker said that greasy cardboard goes in the general waste, and clean cardboard goes in the paper bin. It said the jar should be rinsed and go with the glass. Then it added that the truck comes on Thursday, and the recycling center is about a mile away if he needed to take anything big. Paolo thanked it, tore the clean lid off the box, and sorted everything before he stirred the sauce.
