First aid is what you do right away when someone gets a small injury, before a doctor can help. For a small burn, you hold the skin under cool running water for about ten minutes. A stream of cold water from the tap is best. For a small cut, you press a clean cloth on it until the bleeding stops. People often ask an assistant for help in the moment, and they say things like, 'My finger is burned, what do I do?' or 'Call an ambulance.' Keep your phone close and working. Stay with the person, and if the pain does not fade in half an hour, call a doctor.

Writing usually starts with a rough draft, and then you edit it. People ask for help with spelling, word counts and small changes. They say, 'How many words is this?', 'Fix the spelling in the last line' or 'Make this sound more cozy.' If a change goes wrong, they say, 'Undo.' Some writers pay for an app that checks their writing. If they do not like it, they can cancel and ask for a refund. Most of the time, though, writing is just a person, a page and a few good words.

The assistant said a small plant or a box of tea would be a good gift, and named two shops nearby. Youssef picked the tea. The assistant set a reminder for Thursday at five to pick it up. He thanked it, sipped some water, and went back to bed.

Elif sat at her desk and stared at the calendar. Her friend's wedding was coming up, and she kept losing track of the days. 'How many days until June twentieth?' she asked her phone. She felt weak after a long morning, and the cups in the office sink were piling up, but at least the date was clear. 'Remind me one week before,' she said. The assistant set it.

Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't move the cover myself. I can remind you to do it. Do you want that?
Person: ok. and remind me to get test strips at the pharmacy
Assistant: Done. The total is two reminders: the cover on the 5th, and the test strips tomorrow.

Mikko grabbed his coat and ran toward the kitchen. He had a train to catch and a long article to read on the way. 'Excuse me, could you please make my coffee strong and not too sweet? I'm in a hurry, and I have a private call at nine, so I need to be awake for it,' he said to the coffee machine. The machine followed his words. It brewed a strong cup with only one spoon of sugar and said it would take two minutes. Mikko tapped his foot. When the light turned green, he poured the coffee into his travel cup, said thanks, and was out the door.

A washing machine cleans clothes with water and soap, and a dryer dries them with warm air. Most machines have programs: a short wash for a few clothes, a long one for dirty towels. People change the program by saying, 'Do a quick wash,' 'Make the water colder,' or 'Dry on low heat.' When the weather is rainy, many people use the dryer instead of a line outside. Before a trip, they pack clean clothes, so they ask, 'When will the load be done?' The assistant tells them how many minutes are left.

A video meeting lets people at different desks talk together. You join with a link or by saying, 'Join my ten o'clock call.' Before it starts, an agenda lists what everyone will talk about. People share their screen so others can see slides, and they often say, 'Share my screen,' 'Mute me,' or 'Turn off my camera.' Sit near a window or a lamp so your face has a soft glow, and keep your desk clean so the background looks tidy. If you work at a shared station in a busy office, you can ask for a quiet room before the call begins.

Tomas sat in his reading chair with a book, but the room felt too bright and harsh. The dryer was humming in the next room as it finished a load of towels. 'It's like a hospital in here,' he said to the smart speaker. The assistant understood that the lights were too strong. It lowered the ceiling light to thirty percent and changed the bulb to a warm color. Tomas smiled. 'A little less white, and maybe something blue by the window?' The assistant changed the lamp by the window to a soft blue. 'Perfect,' said Tomas, and he turned the page.

Kofi was feeding his baby when he spotted a bill on the table. The shiny new bank card had come in the mail, but he needed to move some money first. 'How much is in my savings?' he asked. The assistant said there was four hundred dollars in savings and nine hundred in checking. 'Move half of my savings to checking,' he said. The assistant moved two hundred dollars from savings to checking and said the new balance in checking was eleven hundred. Kofi nodded. He also asked it to remind him to pay the cable bill on Friday. The assistant set the reminder. Kofi wiped the baby's chin and went back to feeding.

Clocks show what time it is where you are, but the world has many time zones. When it is noon in London, it is seven in the morning in New York. People who call family far away often check the time first, because nobody wants to wake a friend at night. They say, 'What time is it in Tokyo?' or 'Is it too late to call Sam in Sydney?' Some people hate doing the math in their head, and they are lucky to have a watch or phone that does it for them. When they travel, they can also say, 'Change my clock to local time.'

A text message is a short note you send to someone's phone. People write one to a friend, or to a group chat with many people. When you cannot type, you can say, 'Text Mia I am running late,' and your phone writes and sends it. You can also ask, 'Read my new messages' or 'Reply sorry, I can't come.' A delivery driver who earns tips by the hour cannot hold a phone, so they talk to it. If you will be late to the theater, a quick text saves a lot of worry. And before it goes out, you can say, 'Change it to nine thirty.'

Tessa woke up to a strange noise outside. It sounded like a dog crying. The house was cold, and she did not want to go out in her slippers. 'Brr, my feet are ice,' she said to the speaker. The assistant understood and turned the heat up to twenty-one degrees. Then Tessa asked, 'Has anyone posted about a missing dog?' The assistant checked the neighborhood board and said a neighbor had posted that a brown dog named Ocean had been missing since last night. Tessa put on her coat and boots, grabbed a leash, and went out to look for him.

Kwame sat in the corner of the library with a history essay due on Friday. His shirt for tomorrow's presentation needed an iron too, but that could wait. 'Don't set a reminder for tonight,' he told his phone. 'I don't want to be bothered until after dinner.' The assistant said okay, no reminders tonight. 'Instead, remind me tomorrow at seven to iron my shirt.' The assistant set it. Kwame opened a sweet snack, a peanut butter bar, and went back to the essay. Then he asked, 'How many days until the essay is due?' The assistant said three days.

name: fridge_stock_check
does: Tells you which food in the fridge is running low, puts it on the shopping list, and reminds you to wash fruit when you bring it home.
inputs: the names of the foods, even silly nicknames like the fizzy stuff, and how low the level should be before it warns you
people say:
- Are we out of milk?
- What's running low in the kitchen?
- Do we have any eggs left?
- I think we need more apples
- What should I buy this week?
- Is there still cheese in the fridge?

name: screen_time_helper
does: Sets how long a child can use a tablet each day, up to a maximum, and can unlock extra time as a reward for a good grade or finished chores.
inputs: the child's name, the number of minutes, and the reason for extra time
people say:
- Give Leo another half hour tonight
- No more tablet for Mia today
- She got a good grade, so let her play a bit longer
- How long has he been on the screen?
- Stop the games after dinner
- Let them watch one more show

A smart lock lets you open or close your front door without a key. It is for safety, and for letting people in when you are not home. People who travel often feel nervous about leaving the door open, so they ask, 'Did I lock the door?' or 'Lock up the house.' You can also say, 'Let my neighbor in at three' or 'Who is at the door?' A camera by the door shows the path, the tree by the gate and any visitor or delivery person. When the garage door is open, you can say, 'Close the garage.'

A morning drink is a small ritual. Coffee, tea and smoothies can be made stronger, weaker or sweeter, and people tell the machine or the assistant what they like. They say, 'Make it stronger,' 'Less sugar,' 'A little more milk' or 'Hot, not warm.' Someone who feels hungry may ask for a smoothie with banana and oats. If you are stuck in traffic and worry about being late, you might ask for a quick tea at the next stop. It is the little changes, a bit more here and a bit less there, that make a drink yours.

When you order food for delivery, a restaurant cooks the meal and a driver brings it to you. The app shows how long it will take. Hungry people often ask, 'Where is my order?' or 'How long now?' You can change things too: 'No onions,' 'Make it two burgers,' or 'Leave it at the door.' A tip is a thank you to the driver, and many people say, 'Tip ten percent.' When the food comes, you unpack the bag and check it. Some people write a personal note like, 'Ring twice, the baby sleeps.' The app may also send news about delays.

Nathan sat in his office chair and needed quiet music to focus. He had an urgent report to finish. 'Play something calm,' he said to his phone. The assistant started a playlist of soft piano. Just then he had to sneeze, and the music seemed too loud. 'A little lower,' he said, and the volume went down. 'And at quarter to ten, pause the music, please. I have a call.' The assistant said it would pause the music at quarter to ten. Nathan nodded, typed the last page of the report, and reached for a tissue.

The person wants to be reminded when the baby's next feeding is due, so there is fresh milk ready, even on a busy day at the mall or on a zoom call.
When is the next feeding?
Remind me to feed the baby at three
Baby's bottle time, what is it?
I don't remember when she last ate
Tell me when she last ate and remind me for the next one
How long until the baby needs a bottle?
Could you please remind me about the next feeding and tell me when she last ate?
Feed time?

Wiremu was fixing a fan when the house got hotter. He had a screw in one hand and a toddler on his lap. 'Turn on the air conditioning, but not in the baby's room,' he said. The assistant turned on the cooling in the living room and left the nursery alone. The thermostat was offline for a moment, so the assistant waited and then set it to twenty-three degrees. 'Don't make it too cold,' Wiremu added. He swiped on his phone to check the temperature. It showed twenty-six, and falling. He put down the screw and relaxed.

Sofia had moved to a new city, and she did not know the buses yet. Her sister would call at six, and Sofia expected a serious talk about money. 'Could you please remind me at half past five to leave work? I'm still learning the buses, and I don't want to be late for my sister's call,' she said. The assistant set a reminder for half past five and said it would ring twice. 'Also, remind me when I get near the corner shop to buy milk.' The assistant said it would remind her when she was nearby. Sofia smiled, shut her laptop and started to pack her bag.

Many older people live alone, and their families like to know they are safe. A check-in call is a short chat each day. If the person does not answer, the family gets a message. Medicine reminders say when to take a pill. If something goes wrong, like a fall, the person can say, 'Call for help,' and the phone calls a nearby neighbor or an ambulance. People also say, 'Call my daughter' or 'Remind me about my pills at eight.' They try not to break their routine, and an invitation to tea at a neighbor's house can be a good reminder too.

Person: Find me a funny movie and tell me when it plays tonight.
Assistant: Which cinema should I check?
Person: The one near the market. I'm busy in the kitchen, so please type the times on my phone. My gram wants to come too.
Assistant: The cinema near the market has a comedy at 7:15 and at 9:30.
Person: Can you buy tickets for the early one?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't buy tickets. I can open their website for you.
Person: Okay, do that. And remind me to leave at 6:30.
Assistant: The website is open, and your reminder is set for 6:30.

A robot vacuum drives around the floor and picks up dust by itself. It is for people who don't have time to sweep. You can change how it works: 'Clean the kitchen only,' 'Clean at ten every morning,' or 'Use medium suction.' Some robots can't climb over a thing above a certain height, like a thick rug. Before guests come, many people invite the robot to run: 'Vacuum before my friends arrive.' When it is done, it goes back to its charger. 'Stop cleaning' or 'Go home' calls it back.

Walter was texting his friends while he sat in class. Ten people wanted to meet at the park on Saturday, but his calendar looked full. 'How many things do I have on Saturday?' he asked. The assistant said he had three: soccer at nine, a haircut at noon, and dinner with his aunt. Everything blue on his calendar was school stuff, and there was none on Saturday. 'Move the haircut to Sunday,' he said. The assistant moved it. He wanted to decrease the time soccer took, so he said, 'Make soccer half an hour shorter.' The assistant changed it to end at nine thirty. Walter texted his friends: see you at the park at ten.

Person: can u stop the watr, there is a small leak
Assistant: Do you want me to close the main valve for the whole house or only the kitchen line?
Person: just kitchen, the kids are in the bath
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can only close the main valve, not the kitchen line. The bath would lose water too.
Person: ok wait. there is sand in the water too
Assistant: Sand in the water can mean a problem with a pipe or the water heater. I would call a plumber. Do you want me to call one?
Person: yes please
Assistant: Calling a plumber now. I'll tell them about the leak and the sand.

name: chore_chart_keeper
does: Keeps a daily chore chart for the family, like clearing the table or tidying the corner of the room where the toys live, and lets kids swap jobs.
inputs: the child's name, the chore, and the day
people say:
- Who does the dishes today?
- Let me and Ben trade jobs
- Put Ella on trash duty tomorrow
- What are my chores today?
- Mark my room as done
- Is it Sam's turn to set the table?

Zana was a retired teacher, and her dad was coming to visit that afternoon. 'Could you please start the robot vacuum in the living room and the hall now? My dad is coming at three, and dust makes him cough,' she said politely. The assistant started the robot and said it would finish in about forty minutes. It was hot in the house, so Zana asked the assistant to turn on the fan. It did. Then she said, 'Turn off the vacuum at two thirty, please.' The assistant set that. Zana poured a cold glass of water and waited for the sound of the robot to stop.

Diego was in the kitchen cooking a big dinner, and his cousin was waiting on a video call from Lisbon. He poured a little wine into the sauce and stirred. 'I hope it's not too late for my cousin,' he said to his speaker. The assistant understood and said it was ten at night local time in Lisbon, and five in the afternoon where Diego was. 'A bit late, but still okay for a call,' it said. Diego smiled, turned the heat down under the pot, and pressed the call button. His cousin's face came up on the screen, already in pajamas.

Pooja finished her homework and sat on the sofa. 'There's nothing to watch and I'm so bored,' she said to her phone. The assistant understood that she wanted a film, and it listed three movies at the cinema nearby tonight, including a travel adventure. She picked the adventure. 'Is there a show after six?' she asked. The assistant said there was one at seven thirty. Pooja looked at her shoes, which were dirty from the park. 'I'd better change,' she said. She asked the assistant to remind her to buy candy at the shop on the way, and it did.

name: walk_tracker
does: Counts steps, distance and pace on a walk or run, shows the result on a smart mirror, and can send a short tweet with the result.
inputs: when you start and stop, a goal such as five kilometers, and whether to share the result
people say:
- How many steps have I done today?
- Start tracking my run
- How far did I go this morning?
- Am I faster than yesterday?
- Tell my friends I did five kilometers
- Did I reach my goal?

A reminder is a small note that rings at a time or place so you do not forget. People use them for pills, birthdays, or taking out the rubbish. You can say, 'Remind me at five to call Mom,' or 'Remind me when I get home to water the plants.' The sound is sharp so you notice it. If a reminder comes at the wrong time, say 'Snooze ten minutes' or 'Change it to six.' To start fresh, you can reset it or clear all of them. A note on the sink that says wash the cups is a reminder too.

Aminata sat in her quiet kitchen with the tablet on the table. Autumn had come, and her old winter coat no longer fit her. Last week she had ordered a new one online, but it came in size large and was far too big. She tapped the little microphone and said, "Swap coat."
The assistant opened her recent orders and found the coat. "Do you want a medium instead?" it asked. "Yes, medium," said Aminata. The assistant started an exchange, put a return label on the screen, and told her the courier would collect the big coat on Thursday. It also said the medium one would arrive in about five days.
Aminata smiled. She had not needed to call the shop or find her glasses to read the small print. She put the tablet down and went to make a cup of tea.

Li ran a small kitchen shop, and on Monday morning she had a video call with a supplier about a new blender. She said to her phone, "Please join my ten o'clock call and share my screen with the price list." The phone did both. It opened the call link, and a moment later the price list showed on the screen for everyone.
The supplier was polite and let her speak first. Halfway through, a customer walked into the shop and Li had to step away. "Pause the screen share for now," she said, and the assistant paused it.
When she came back she said, "Resume the share." The list appeared again and the supplier nodded. At the end of the call Li said, "Thanks, that's all. Stop sharing and leave the call." The assistant closed the call, and her phone went back to the sales sheet for the day.

Someone who is grilling dinner before a trip, with a large bag packed and a ticket bought in a sale, wants to know if the flight is late.
Is my flight late?
Any delay on flight 482?
Is it delayed by more than an hour?
Will the plane leave on time or later than planned?
how late is the Lisbon flight
Has my departure moved back by half an hour or more?
Is the wait twice as long as it was this morning?
Could you please check whether my flight to Rome is running behind schedule?
I'd like to know if I have more time than I thought before I need to be at the gate.

A contact is a small card in your phone with a person's name, number, address and birthday. People keep contacts so they do not have to remember every number. Most changes are small. A friend gets a new phone, so you say, "Change Sam's number to 555 0142." A cousin moves house, so you say, "Update Rosa's address." You can also add a note, like "Likes honey cake," to help you remember a gift. If the assistant finds two people with the same name, it asks which one, and you can point to the right one on the screen. Many people add a birthday to each card, because a friend will be glad you remembered the day. When someone is no longer in your life, you can simply say, "Delete that contact."

name: daily_agenda_maker
does: Writes a short agenda for a meeting, folds small topics together so the meeting stays short, and sends it to everyone before the daily check-in.
inputs: the meeting time, the list of topics, and who is invited, for example a team or a visiting artist
people say:
- Make a plan for tomorrow's meeting
- Can you put together what we will talk about at ten?
- I need a list of topics for our team call
- Write up the agenda and send it to everyone
- Draw up an outline for the call with the design team

Person: I'm busy with my polymer clay pots today. Please set a timer for them.
Assistant: Happy to. How many minutes should I set it for?
Person: The block of clay says they should bake for eleven minutes.
Assistant: Done. The timer is set for eleven minutes, and I will tell you when it ends.
Person: Lovely. Could you also paint the pots for me?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't paint. But I can remind you to paint them when they have cooled. Would you like that?
Person: Yes, remind me in one hour.
Assistant: Okay, I will remind you in one hour.

Person: need a new guest wifi pasword pls
Assistant: Of course. How long should it last, one day or one week?
Person: just today. a pair of clients are coming at two
Assistant: Done. The new password works until midnight, and the router will beep once when it is ready. Should I send it to your phone?
Person: yes. and tell me the exact speed too
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't run a speed test from here. I can send you the password now, though.
Person: ok thanks, send it
Assistant: Sent. It is on your phone.

Someone driving with a kid in the back on a dry day wants to know how long the trip will take, and whether another road is quicker.
How long is the drive?
Hang on, is there a faster way to get there?
What's the time to Gran's house?
Will we get there sooner if I take the back road?
How much longer until we arrive?
Is there a route that saves ten minutes?
Could you tell me if the other road is half as slow as this one?
I'd like to know how long the trip home will take, and if a quicker way exists.
Is traffic worse than usual, or will we be there in under an hour?

Laura stood at the stove with flour on her hands. A spider was walking along the window above the sink, but she had no time for it. The soup was cooked, the bread was nearly done, and her guests were coming at seven.
Her phone buzzed on the shelf. It was a missed call from her brother Marco. "Call Marco back," she said, "but not on speaker, the kitchen is too loud." The assistant dialled his number and kept the call quiet.
Marco did not answer. "Do you want to leave a voicemail?" asked the assistant.
"No voicemail," said Laura. "Just send him a text. Say I will call after dinner."
The assistant typed the words, read them back to her, and sent the text. Laura nodded and went back to her bread.

name: pick_up_where_left
does: Is a patient helper that finds the spot where a listener stopped in a podcast or audiobook and starts playing again from there.
inputs: the name of the show or book, such as a call-in radio show, a podcast about grilling, or a long novel
people say:
- Pick up my book where I left off
- Where did I stop in the history podcast?
- Keep going with the story from last night
- Play the rest of that episode
- Start the cooking show again from where it stopped

On a warm evening in June, Sara burned her finger on a hot oven tray. She was a retired teacher and she did not panic, but she did not want to guess either. She spoke to her tablet. "Excuse me, could you please tell me what to do for a small burn on my finger? I live alone, and I would like to be sure I do the right thing before I eat my dinner."
The assistant told her to hold the burn under cool running water for ten minutes, and not to use ice or butter. It set a ten minute timer for her. When the timer rang, it asked if the skin was blistered. "No, just red," said Sara. The assistant said she could cover it with a clean, loose bandage. It also said to see a doctor if the pain got stronger. Sara thanked it and sat down to eat.

Dong-hyun was late for class and walked fast across the yard. He took out his phone and typed with his thumb, "wheres my order, i need it befor friday".
The assistant looked at his online orders. He had bought a big bag of baking sugar and a pair of cheap headphones. It said the sugar was out for delivery and would arrive by four o'clock. The headphones were stuck in a bad storm and would come on Thursday.
"Thursday is fine," Dong-hyun said to himself. "Chill, it's not a problem." Then he typed, "leave the sugar with the front desk". The assistant sent a note to the courier with that request and told him it was done.
Dong-hyun put his phone away and ran into class just as the bell rang.

Someone wants the air conditioning on and the house mild again by this evening.
Cool the house a bit
AC on, please
Can you make the living room cooler by seven tonight?
It's too hot in here
Please help me cool down the bedroom before bed on Friday evening
I want the whole house mild when I get home at six
Turn the fan on low until the afternoon
Could you set the air conditioning to come on tomorrow morning at eight?

name: dough_rise_timer
does: Sets a timer for rising dough, tells you when it is ready for the oven, and reminds you to paint the top with egg before baking, even if you can only give a rough guess of the room's warmth.
inputs: the kind of dough, how warm the kitchen is, and where it is resting, even if it is on a towel on the couch
people say:
- How long does my bread dough need to rise?
- Is the dough ready for the oven yet?
- Start a timer for the dough, it's a cold kitchen today
- Remind me when the pizza dough has doubled
- Tell me when to shape the loaves

A shopping list helps you remember what to buy so you do not stand in the shop and wonder. Most people keep it on their phone and tell the assistant what to put on it. They say "Add milk" or "We are out of eggs." Some people take a picture of the fridge, so they can see what is missing. Others ask the assistant to convert a recipe into a list, with each thing in one line. When the list changes, people say "Take bread off" or "Put two apples on." One family has a funny rule: anything that runs out goes on the list that same day. That way nobody opens an empty box of cereal on Monday morning.

Zofia had lived in the city for only a week. She came home and found a card on her door. It said a parcel was waiting at the post office, and nobody had been there to sign for it.
She sighed and spoke to her phone. "I'm never home when the courier comes, and I can't afford to lose this one. It's my winter coat."
The assistant understood. It showed her the nearest post office, which was ten minutes away and open until six. It said she could be back from work by half past five, in time to collect it. Then it asked, "Would you like to make a permanent change, so that parcels go to a pickup point near your office?"
"Yes, please," said Zofia. The assistant saved the new address and set a reminder to collect the coat at five thirty.

Silvia never liked her phone. One afternoon she came out of the shop with a heavy box in her arms and could not remember where she had parked. She stood in the car park and said, loudly, "Where is my car, and is the tyre pressure okay?"
The assistant answered both. The car was on level two, in row C, and the pressure was fine on three tyres, but the rear left was a little low. Silvia had guessed something was wrong, because the car pulled to one side that morning.
The assistant also said the car park charged hourly, and she had been there for two hours. "It will cost six euros," it said. Silvia thanked it, found her car, and put the box in the back. She drove to the garage to fill the tyre.

Sven woke up and rubbed his eyes. Last night a screw had fallen out of his bookshelf, and now one side hung crooked. He sat up on the edge of the bed and said to his phone, "Order the same screws as last time, but not the long ones. I don't want to drill any deeper."
The assistant looked at his last order and found a box of short wood screws. It added them to the basket and asked, "Should I send them to your home address?" Sven said yes.
The assistant placed the order and said it would arrive tomorrow. Then it offered to follow the delivery and tell him when the parcel was close. "Good idea," Sven mumbled, and fell back onto his pillow for ten more minutes.

Emi stood in the empty living room, surrounded by boxes. The wind rattled the window and the street outside was snowy and quiet. The kids zoomed down the hall with their toy cars while she held her phone.
"The movers come on Friday, and I don't think anyone has told the power company," she said.
The assistant understood that this was a request. It found the power company on her list and asked, "Do you want to stop the service at this address on Friday and start it at your new address?" Emi said yes and gave the new street.
The assistant sent the form, and a note appeared on the screen to say the change was booked. Emi put a tick on her list and picked up another box.

Person: It's too bright in the bedroom. I just got home from work.
Assistant: I can help. How dim should the lights be? They are at fifty percent now.
Person: Half of that, please.
Assistant: Done. The bedroom lights are at twenty-five percent.
Person: Thanks. I spent twelve hours on my feet. Could you turn off the kitchen light too? I think I left it on when I cooked last night.
Assistant: Yes, the kitchen light is off now.
Person: Now can you sweep the hall with the broom?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't sweep. I only control the lights and the speakers. Would you like a reminder to sweep after you rest?
Person: Yes, tomorrow at noon.

Person: Excuse me, could you please remind me to call my mother on Sunday? I moved here last month and I keep forgetting, and I know she misses me.
Assistant: Of course. What time on Sunday should I remind you?
Person: Around six in the evening. She lives far to the east, so that is a good hour for her too.
Assistant: Okay. I will remind you on Sunday at six. What should I name the reminder?
Person: Please name it "Call Mom".
Assistant: Done. The reminder "Call Mom" is set for Sunday at six in the evening.

Person: Please find us a room in Lisbon for three nights.
Assistant: Sure. How many guests will there be, and which night do you arrive?
Person: Two adults and two kids. Sorry, make that three kids, I forgot my niece. We arrive on the ninth of May.
Assistant: Got it: two adults, three kids, one big family room, from the ninth of May. Shall I show the choices?
Person: Yes, but I can't click on the little buttons while I hold the baby. Can you read them out and turn the volume up? The kids are loud.
Assistant: The volume is up. The first room is a big family room with two beds and a sofa bed. It costs ninety euros a night.
Person: That sounds good. Take that one.

name: room_heating_plan
does: Sets, changes or cancels a heating plan for one room, so it is warm when people are at home.
inputs: which room, for example the south bedroom or the room with the sofa, the temperature you want, and the time
people say:
- Warm up the south bedroom by seven
- Keep the sofa room cozy tonight
- Stop the morning heat for tomorrow
- I'm cold, can you turn the radiator on in the hall?
- Don't heat the house while we're away this weekend

Mai was babysitting her little cousin, who had finally fallen asleep. It had taken an hour, and she felt as if she had won a game. She sat at the computer to finish her homework, with the baby monitor beside her.
She typed to her phone, "baby monitor is so quiet, i can barely hear anything".
The assistant understood what she meant. The monitor volume was at the minimum, so it raised the volume to a middle level and said, "I turned the monitor up. Can you hear the baby breathing now?"
"Yes, I can," Mai said. She also asked when the baby had last eaten. The assistant checked the feeding log and said it was at five o'clock, so the next feed would be around eight. Mai set a reminder and went back to her homework.

Odile got home at eight in the morning with her eyes burning from the bright lights at the hospital. She was a nurse, and she had been awake all night. Before she lay down, she spoke to the smart speaker on the shelf.
"Post in the neighborhood group that the garden sale is on the first of May," she said. "Then turn off my notifications until four this afternoon."
The assistant wrote the post and read it back: "Garden sale on the first of May. Come and say hello!" Odile said it was fine, and the assistant sent it to the group. Then it silenced the notifications from her social media apps until four.
"Thank you," Odile whispered. She pulled the curtains and slept without a single buzz from her phone.

Tunde woke up late. Rain drummed on the roof, and his clock said ten past eight. He grabbed his phone and mumbled two words, "Route to work?"
The assistant looked at the traffic. There was an accident on the main road, which meant a long wait. It offered a small road along the river instead. "That way takes twenty-five minutes," it said. "The main road takes fifty."
"River road," said Tunde. The assistant started the directions, and the phone read the first turn out loud while he pulled on his shoes. He ran to the car, still half asleep, and followed the quiet voice all the way to his office. He arrived five minutes before his first meeting.

Someone wants the dog fed now, in the tidy bowl by the front door, with a slice of apple on the side.
Feed the dog
Dinner time for Max
Max is staring at his empty bowl
It's past his usual dinner time, I think
Can you put out the dog's food now, please?
He has been walking around the kitchen for an hour
Please open the feeder so he can eat
I'd like the dog to have his dinner before we leave, if you could start it
My dog looks very hungry

name: pantry_stock_counter
does: Counts the cans, boxes and bottles in the pantry and the fridge, and lists what is running low, with a bigger check for the yearly clean-out, so you do not need a midnight trip to the shop.
inputs: the room or shelf to check, and the least amount of each thing you want to keep
people say:
- What are we running out of?
- How many eggs are left?
- Do we have any rice?
- Check the pantry before I go shopping
- Is the milk almost gone?

A focus timer helps you work hard for a short time and then rest. A common routine is twenty-five minutes of work and five minutes of break. The idea is to keep your mind fresh, so you do not stare at the screen for hours. People use the breaks to stand up, drink water, or charge their phone. Many people change the timer to fit them. They say, "Make the work part longer," "Shorten my break," or "Start a timer for forty minutes." Some people narrow their goal to one task, like "Focus on my report until noon." A traveler waiting at the airport can use the same routine to answer emails, one short block at a time.

Aarav, a retired teacher, was packing for a trip. His taxi was coming in a small amount of time, so he tidied the hall in a hurry and picked up his bag. He turned to the smart lock and said, "Lock the front door, but don't lock the garage. My son needs to get his tools this afternoon."
The assistant locked the front door and left the garage open. "Do you want me to close the garage later?" it asked.
"Yes, please," said Aarav. "Remind me at five to check it is closed."
The assistant set a reminder for five o'clock. Aarav heard the taxi horn outside, picked up his bag, and walked to the car. The door clicked behind him, locked and safe.

Many people forget birthdays, so they ask the assistant to keep the dates for them. You say, "Remember that my sister's birthday is on the third of June," and a few days before, the assistant reminds you. It can also help with gift ideas. If a friend loves to dance, you might ask, "What can I give someone who loves dance?" The assistant may suggest a class or a pair of good shoes. People change things all the time. They say, "Move the reminder to a week before," or "Sit down with me and write a card." Some people pick a card with a red ribbon, others choose a plain white one. Either way, the assistant helps the day feel easy.

Marisa ran a small cafe, and her pea soup was the most popular dish on the menu. Today a school group had booked lunch, and she needed to make the soup for forty people. Her recipe made only four bowls.
She wiped her hands and said to her phone, "My recipe makes four bowls. Make it enough for forty, and set a timer for twenty minutes so I remember to start the oven."
The assistant multiplied every amount by ten and read them out: ten cups of peas, five onions, and ten spoons of salt. Marisa also asked how much the extra peas would cost, but the assistant said it did not know the prices at her shop. It set the timer for twenty minutes.
Marisa nodded, took out her biggest pot, and added a purple cabbage salad to the day's menu.

Someone who booked a game night wants to know the score of a board game, where one sad player is far behind and the tiles are in a basket.
What's the score?
Who is winning?
How many points is Dan ahead?
Am I behind by more than ten?
Tell me everyone's totals
Is it close, or is someone way ahead?
How many more points do I need to catch up?
Could you please read out the score for each player, from the most points to the least?

Joost was unpacking boxes in his shop when he remembered his uncle's medicine. The nurse had said Uncle Piet should take his pills at noon and weigh himself every morning. Joost's hands were full of coat hangers, so he typed fast on his phone.
"remind my uncle to take his pils at noon and call me if he doesnt answer"
The assistant understood the whole message. At noon it spoke through the speaker in Uncle Piet's kitchen, in a friendly, personal way: "Time for your pills, Uncle Piet." Uncle Piet did not answer, so the assistant called Joost. Joost laughed and said, "He is in the garden again." He phoned his uncle's mobile himself. Uncle Piet picked up on the third ring, and the pills were taken ten minutes late.

Most people have a usual drink. It might be coffee with one sugar, or tea with a splash of milk. A machine or an assistant can make it the same way each morning, so you do not have to think about it. People often change how strong or sweet the drink is. They say, "Make it stronger," "Increase the sugar by one spoon," or "A little less milk, please." On a cold day they may ask for something fancy, like a latte with foam. In summer they may ask for an iced tea, poured from a can or made fresh. A good habit is to taste the drink first, and then tell the assistant what to change.

Person: Please call Anna.
Assistant: Which Anna? I have Anna Brown and Anna Lopez.
Person: Anna Brown. No, wait, I mean Anna Lopez, from the hotel.
Assistant: Calling Anna Lopez now.
Person: My glasses are foggy and I cannot read the screen. Did anyone call me this morning?
Assistant: Yes, there were two missed calls. One was from your son, and one from the doctor's office. Shall I read the voicemail?
Person: Yes, the one from my son. The phone flashed, but I did not hear it ring.
Assistant: Playing it now.

Kenji had ten minutes before his train and his bag was already on his shoulder. He called out to the speaker, "Set the pool to twenty-eight degrees by this evening."
"Should I start the heater now?" asked the assistant.
"No, at four o'clock," said Kenji. "Not before."
The assistant set the heater for four. Then it scanned the pool sensors and said, "The pump battery is low, but everything else is working well. The water is twenty-three degrees now."
"Thanks," said Kenji. "Remind me to change the battery tomorrow." The assistant made a note, and Kenji ran out of the door just as the train began to roll into the station.

Dana walked out of the hospital after a long night shift and put her earbuds in. The coffee in her bag was stale, and all she wanted was a shower. She spoke to her phone in a low voice.
"text mom im on my way home, wil have breakfast there"
The assistant turned her words into a message and read it back: "Mom, I'm on my way home, will have breakfast there." Dana nodded, and the assistant sent it.
A moment later her mom replied that she was making pancakes. The assistant read the answer into her earbuds. Dana smiled, asked it to shift her alarm for the afternoon to four o'clock, and walked slowly to the bus stop.

Zoe stood at the front of the meeting room, under the big tv. She had to update the numbers for the sales sheet, and her head was full of figures. She spoke to her phone.
"Add up one hundred twenty, eighty and forty-five, and tell me if that is more than two hundred fifty."
The assistant said the total was two hundred forty-five. "That is five less than two hundred fifty," it added.
Zoe nodded. "Now take half of it." The assistant answered one hundred twenty-two and a half. Zoe typed the numbers into the sheet, checked them once on the screen, and pressed save. The meeting started two minutes later, and the sheet was ready.

Person: book a tabel for tonight
Assistant: Happy to. For how many people, and at what time?
Person: 4 at 7. nothing too pricey, i can't afford a fancy place
Assistant: Understood. What kind of food would you like?
Person: anything with deep dish pizza
Assistant: There is a pizza place five minutes from your office with a table for four at seven. Shall I book it?
Person: yes please. also is there a hardware shop open near there? my chair has a loose screw
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't search for shops. I can only help with restaurants. Your table is booked.

Taras closed his shop for the night and sat on the couch with a bowl of pea soup. He was tired and wanted something simple to watch. He lifted his phone and said, "Movies nearby?"
The assistant listed three films at the cinema around the corner, with times. One was a comedy at eight. "The comedy," said Taras.
The assistant showed the trailer and asked if he wanted to buy a ticket. "Not yet," said Taras. "First, connect to the living room tv." The assistant connected the phone to the tv, and the trailer played on the big screen. Taras laughed twice, then said, "Buy one ticket." The assistant did it, and Taras finished his soup.

Camille was proud of the new painting in her hall. It was a perfect spring day, and the garden had begun to grow. She did not like technology, but her son had put a smart lock on the front door and told her to just talk to it.
Before she left for the market, she said, "Is my front door locked? I think I left it open longer than usual this week."
The assistant said the door had been unlocked for almost two hours, which was twice as long as usual. "Do you want me to lock it now?" it asked.
"Yes, please," said Camille. The lock clicked. She smiled, picked up her basket, and walked down the street with a lighter heart.

Person: I just got home from work and my brain is mush. My sister's birthday is on Saturday.
Assistant: Would you like some gift ideas, or a reminder?
Person: Ideas, please. She has dreamed of a garden for years, but she only has the flat upstairs from mine.
Assistant: A window box with herb seeds would be a nice gift. How much would you like to spend?
Person: Not sure. Maybe twenty euros?
Assistant: That is enough for a long box, soil and three kinds of seeds. Shall I remind you to buy it?
Person: Yes, tomorrow at five. I'll park by the garden store on my way home.

Someone excited about a dinner party wants to scale a recipe up for twelve people, so the meal will shine, and they can't nail the maths alone.
Make this recipe for twelve
Double it, and tell me the new amounts
Scale the cake to eight slices and list the cups and spoons
I need this soup to feed twelve, so change the amounts and the number of servings
Cut it in half and tell me how many it serves
Can you make it bigger, and write the new list in cups?
Please turn this recipe into one for six, and read the amounts out loud
I'd like to triple the sauce and also know how many people it will feed

Someone wants a plan for what to cook this week, with a good balance of foods, after a snowy weekend of eating badly and wanting to practice cooking at home more.
What should I cook this week?
Plan my dinners for the week
Give me five healthy dinners
The fridge is empty and I'm tired of takeout
I don't know what to eat all week
Could you make a menu for seven days with fish, beans and vegetables?
It's freezing outside and I want warm food every night
I'd like a simple plan for packed lunches too, if that's not too much trouble

Edward sat by his pool on a warm day. The sun was shining in a clear sky, and the water looked a little cold. He was a grandparent now, and his grandchildren were coming to swim in the afternoon. He lifted his phone and said, "Pool temperature?"
The assistant answered, "The water is twenty degrees."
"Warmer," said Edward.
The assistant asked how warm he wanted it. "Twenty-six," he said. The assistant turned on the electric heater and said it would take about three hours. Edward sat back with his book. When the children arrived, the water was just right, and the little ones jumped in with a happy shout.

Isaac sat on the sofa with a cup of coffee that tasted cold. His kids were asleep, and the pale glow of the tablet screen hurt his eyes. He had been working late all week and wanted one quiet night.
"Turn on a blue light filter, and put the phone on do not disturb until Friday morning," he said.
The assistant made the screen warmer and dimmer. Then it silenced the calls and messages. "Only calls from your family will come through," it said. "Is that all right?"
"Yes, thank you," said Isaac. He finished his coffee, went upstairs, and slept for nine hours without a single beep.

Paolo stared out the airport window. It was snowing hard, and the silver planes sat very still on the ground. He had his boarding card in one hand and his coffee in the other. The big board above him showed no new news.
He took out his phone. "Gate number?" he asked.
The assistant looked at his flight. "Gate fourteen," it said. "But your flight is delayed by forty minutes, because of the snow."
Paolo sighed. "Tell me when it changes." The assistant said it would. Forty minutes later his phone buzzed, and a message said boarding had begun. Paolo threw his cup in the bin and walked to gate fourteen.

Femke's baby slept badly because the nursery felt stuffy. It was spring, and the pollen was high. She held the baby with one arm and said to the speaker, "Is the air in the nursery okay?"
The assistant answered that the air was dusty and dry. "Would you like me to start the purifier?" it asked.
"Yes, and turn it on every night at eight," said Femke. "Make that a permanent schedule."
The assistant set it up. Then Femke said, "Remind me in two weeks to change the filter." The assistant made a note. Femke later put the old filter in the recycling, and the nursery smelled fresh again.

Putri was minding her shop when she remembered her son's school project. She grabbed her phone and typed fast.
"remind jonas to water his bean plant, it is next to the radiator, project due thrusday"
The assistant read the message and understood it. It sent a note to Jonas's tablet that said, "Please water your bean plant today. The project is due on Thursday." It also set a second reminder for Wednesday evening.
That night Jonas wrote back, "The beans are very funny, one is taller than the rest!" Putri laughed and showed the message to her customers. The assistant saved the due date in her calendar.

Someone wants to know how to say "the dessert is ready, come and eat" in another language.
Translate that into Spanish
how do you say it in French
Give me two or three ways to say it in Italian
What is the German for "come and eat"?
Can you say it in Portuguese, but only half as formal?
I need a nicer, more polite way to say this in Japanese, please
Could you help me tell my grandmother in Polish that the sweet things are waiting? I want to say it right, and a bit longer than just one word.

Abena woke up and her head felt heavy. She rubbed her eyes, picked up her phone and said, "Plan our dinners for this week and make me a shopping list." The assistant asked if anyone in the house had a diet. "No pork, and not too much salt," said Abena. In a moment the screen showed seven dinners, from lentil soup on Monday to fish and rice on Sunday. None of them had pork. Below the menu was a shopping list, sorted by the aisles of her shop. The assistant said the soup would take about one hour to cook, and that it might sound plain but would taste great. Abena smiled. The list looked smooth and tidy, with nothing repeated. She sipped her tea, saved the plan, and asked the assistant to send it to her husband too. It did, and he sent back a thumbs up before she had finished breakfast.

Someone wants a bike route home from their yoga class that is not dark or lonely at night.
Bike route home, lit please
Show me a safe way to ride from the studio to my flat
Which streets have lights for cycling at night?
Give me the name of a cycle path that stays bright after sunset
I would rather not ride through the park in the evening, is there another way?
Find me a route on main roads, I don't like cycling when it's late
Could you please plan a ride home with street lights all the way? My class ends at nine and I get nervous riding alone after sunset.

Femke stood at the front door with a lunchbox in one hand and a school bag in the other. "Remind me to collect my parcel at the post office," she told her phone, "and please don't remind me before four, because I am in meetings until then." The assistant set a reminder for a quarter past four. Femke thought for a second. "I don't want the big post office by the market. The small one on Elm Street is closer." The assistant changed the place on the reminder and showed her the opening hours. Closing time was six. When she came home with the box under her arm, she said, "Mark that as done." The assistant crossed it off her list and asked if she needed anything else. "Not today," said Femke, and she went to make dinner.

Nok was stirring a big pot of soup when a guest from Brazil walked into the kitchen. "How do you say welcome in Portuguese, and can you spell it for me?" she asked her phone. The assistant said "bem-vindo" out loud and spelled it letter by letter. Nok wrote it on a card and put it at the front of the menu board. The guest had just won a prize at the food fair, so Nok wanted to learn a few more words. She asked the assistant to show only the words about food, and it filtered the list down to soup, rice, bread and water. Nok practised each one while the soup bubbled. When the guest sat down, she said "bem-vindo" with a big smile, and he laughed and clapped.

A phone's contact list is a small book of people. It is for finding a number or an address fast, so you do not have to remember it. People change their contacts all the time. They say, "Save this number for Dana," or "Change Grandma's address, she moved," or "Put a birthday on my cousin's card." Some people dress up a contact with a photo or a special ringtone, so the phone shows who is calling. On a foggy morning, when your head is slow, it helps that the assistant can find a name for you. You can also say "Delete the old number" or "Put Dana's work phone first." The list stays tidy that way.

Weather forecasts tell us what the sky will do, so we can plan our day. People look at them to decide if they need a coat, an umbrella or sunscreen. A forecast can change, because the wind may shift in the afternoon and bring rain. People ask, "Will it rain today?" or "How cold is it outside?" or "Do I need a jacket tomorrow?" A sailor may check the wind before tying a rope on a boat, and a gardener may check before hanging washing on a line. Many people read the final forecast just before leaving home. If they want another place, they say, "What about Lisbon?" or "Show me the weekend."

At lunch, Lotte sat at her desk and spoke to her phone. "Could you please tell me how much electricity the house used yesterday? I am asking because last month's bill was very high and I want to be careful this time." The assistant checked the meter and said the house had used fourteen units, which was more than normal. It said the dryer and the oven had been on for a long time. Lotte remembered that her brother had said the wire on the old heater felt loose. "Remind me tonight to call an electrician," she said. The assistant set the reminder. It also said the power company would deliver the next bill on Friday, and offered to tell her the total every evening this week. Lotte said yes and went back to her salad.

Olivia sat in her chair at work and looked at a photo of the vegetables she had chopped for the office party. "This picture is so dark. I can't see any of the colors," she said. The assistant made the photo brighter, and now the red peppers and green onions shone. Olivia was glad. She scrolled to another one, where her team was laughing around the table. "My mum would love to see this," she said, half to herself. The assistant asked if it should send the photo to Mum. "Yes, please, just that one, and put it in the party album too." The assistant sent the photo and saved a copy in the album. A minute later Mum sent back three hearts, and Olivia put her phone down with a big smile.

A birthday list is a way to remember who is turning a year older and when. People keep it in a phone so they never forget a date. It is also for gift ideas: you write a tiny note, like "Sam likes tea," and follow it up when the day comes near. People change the list by saying, "Remind me about Mum's birthday a week before," or "Change Sam's gift to a book," or "Save Leo's phone number so I can text him." Some even ask, "What number birthday is Dad having?" When the date is close, the assistant tells them what is on the list, and they can say, "Buy that one" or "Show me cheaper ideas."

name: print_copies
does: Prints several copies of a document, like a flyer for a salty snack sale or a notice about a snow day, so one page is multiplied into a neat stack.
inputs: the document or file name, how many copies, and which printer to use
people say:
- Print ten of these
- I need twenty copies of the snow day letter for tomorrow
- Run off a few more of that flyer
- Make one for everyone in the class, there are thirty of us
- Can you print this again, five times please?
- Give me a stack of the menu for the party

name: book_time_left
does: Tells you how long it will take to finish a book at your usual speed, so you can plan a snowy weekend of reading.
inputs: the book's title, the page you are on, and how many pages you read in an hour; it does not need the weight of the book or how worn the cover is
people say:
- How long until I finish this book?
- Will I be done with my novel by Sunday?
- How many hours of reading are left?
- I'm on page two hundred, how much more do I have?
- Tell me how long chapter nine will take
- Can I get through this before the trip?

Nandi was a little girl with a piggy bank shaped like a frog. One evening, before going to sleep, she spoke to the tablet in her room. "I don't want to buy sweets this month. Can you help me save for a bike?" The assistant asked how much money she had. "Twelve dollars," said Nandi. The assistant said the bike she liked cost forty dollars, so she needed twenty-eight more. It made a plan: put away four dollars each week, and the bike would be hers in seven weeks. Nandi nodded and asked it to switch off the lamp. The assistant did, and then it saved the plan with a little picture of a bike. "Good night," said Nandi, and she hugged her frog bank.

Kwame was at his desk when his video call froze again. He had tried every route he could think of: moving the cable, standing near the window, even shouting at the screen. At last he spoke to his phone. "Restart the router tonight at midnight, please. And tomorrow, switch the guest network off after the meeting at ten." The assistant set both jobs. It also told him that his local provider had reported slow service in his street, which might be the real problem. Kwame sighed. "Then tell me when it is fixed." The assistant said it would check every hour and send him a message. Kwame leaned back, took a sip of tea, and decided to finish the call on his phone for now.

After a good clean with the broom, someone wants the total of the electricity they have used by the end of the week.
Total power used this week?
how many units have we burned so far
What's our electric bill up to now this week?
Add up the electricity from Monday to today
Is my usage so far this week good, or is it high?
Tell me the total by Sunday night, please
Could you please sum up our energy use for the week so far? I'd like to know before the end of the week so I can change what I do.

Measurements tell us how long, how heavy or how hot something is. In a kitchen, a drawer full of cups and spoons helps, but recipes from other countries use different units. People change them by asking, "How many cups is 250 millilitres?" or "What is 350 degrees Fahrenheit in Celsius?" or "How many pounds is two kilos?" Friends share recipes and plans with numbers like these, and a noisy kitchen is no place to do sums in your head. So people ask out loud: "Turn miles into kilometres," "Make that in inches," or "Give me that in grams." The answer helps them follow the recipe or buy the right amount.

Babies sleep and eat on a rhythm, and parents often keep a simple plan for it. A feeding time says when the next bottle is due, and a nap time says when the baby should be in bed. Many families have a baby monitor too, which lets them hear or see the room from far away. Plans change, so people say, "Move the nap to two o'clock," or "Remind me to feed her in an hour," or "Let me know if he wakes up." On Tuesday the plan may be different from Monday, since the baby grows. It helps to have the times correct, so people say, "Show me today's schedule" or "Change the evening feed."

Someone wants the house cooler after the oven has been on and the kids bathe, but doesn't want it freezing.
Cool the kitchen, but not too much
Don't make it freezing, just a bit cooler
Turn the fan on low, I don't want the loud one
It's roasting in here since I used the oven
Cool down the house to twenty-two, not lower
I don't want the air conditioning on all night, but cool the bedroom before bed
Could you cool the living room for about an hour? It's true that I like it fresh, but I don't want the baby to get cold.

Meera looked out of the kitchen window and frowned. The sky was gray. "I wonder if I'll get soaked on the way home," she said to her phone. The assistant checked the weather and said rain would start at seven. Her ride home takes twenty-five minutes, so it suggested she leave at half past six. Meera nodded and opened the route document her cycling club had sent. She tapped the wrong button and the file filled with strange letters. "Oops, undo that," she said. The assistant undid the last change, and the route came back. It showed the short way along the river. Meera wiped her hands on her apron, thanked the assistant, and went back to her pots, glad to know she would stay dry.

A calendar is where we keep the things we plan to do: meetings, classes, trips and time with friends. It is for seeing what is coming and for finding a free hour. People change it all the time. They say, "Move my dentist visit to Friday," "Cancel the meeting at three," or "Make lunch with Ana go an hour longer." Before a hike in the mountain hills, someone might ask, "Am I free on Saturday morning?" A quiet week with nothing in it is easy to see. Many people also say, "Put a reminder before it starts," so they do not forget. It is simple: if you want to go somewhere, put it on the calendar.

Someone wants a quick sum: a yellow kite costs nineteen dollars, the sale takes ten off, and they don't want to blow their money.
nineteen minus ten
What is nineteen take away ten?
19 less 10?
If something costs nineteen and I save ten, what do I pay?
Subtract ten from nineteen
Quick, nineteen minus ten
Could you work out the price of the kite for me? It says nineteen dollars, and there is a discount of ten dollars.

Text messages are short notes we send from a phone. They are for quick things, like "I'm running late" or "Dinner at seven." Group chats let many people talk at once, such as a family or a team. People often ask the assistant to read a message out loud or to write one back. They say, "Text my mother that I am on my way," "Reply yes," or "Tell the group I'll be there at eight." Sometimes they want to change a message: "Make that shorter" or "Say sorry instead." If you have to wake early, you may say, "Send a text to Sam at six." One short reply is enough most of the time.

Olivia had just moved to the city, and tomorrow was her friend Hana's birthday. She did not know the shops yet. "I need a gift for Hana," she told her phone. "I don't want flowers, because she sneezes around them. And I don't want anything big." The assistant asked how much she wanted to spend. "About twenty dollars." It suggested a small plant, a scarf or a book, and then pulled up a map of three shops near her flat. A scarf in a shop window on Maple Street caught her eye. "Is that one open now?" The assistant said it closed at six, and offered to save a note to have the gift ready by five. Olivia said yes and put on her coat.

Music on a phone or speaker is for filling a room with songs you like. People pick a song, an artist or a playlist, and change the volume or skip a track. In the car, music is easy to control by voice, so hands stay on the wheel and a foot stays near the brake. People say, "Play something calm," "Turn it down," "Skip this one," or "Play my morning playlist." The phone may beep when a new message comes in, and then people say, "Pause the music." When a song makes them glad, they ask, "Play that again" or "More songs like this."

name: bin_day_lookup
does: Tells you which bin goes out on which day at your address, so no one has to cry over a smelly missed pickup, whether it is a home or a small hotel.
inputs: the street address and the kind of waste, like paper, glass, food scraps or general rubbish; the answer is fast
people say:
- Which bin goes out tonight?
- When do they take the glass?
- Is tomorrow a compost day?
- Did I miss the rubbish truck this week?
- Does cardboard go in the blue one?
- What do I put out on Thursday?

name: log_baby_nap
does: Writes down when the baby fell asleep and woke up, so parents can understand the sleep pattern, and shows it on the family's website page.
inputs: the time the baby fell asleep, the time the baby woke up, and a note if you like, such as a dark room or a noisy street
people say:
- She just fell asleep, write that down
- He woke up at three
- How long did the baby nap today?
- Keep track of his sleep for me
- Note that the room was too dark and she cried
- Show me this week's naps

In elderly care, small helpers make life easier and safer. A medicine reminder says when to take a pill, and a check-in call lets a family hear that grandma is fine. For an emergency, a button or a word calls for help. People change these things as needs change: "Remind Dad about his pills at eight," "Call my aunt every morning," or "Bring up the number for the doctor." A notebook by the phone helps too, with names and times written in it. The family wants every time to be correct, so they ask, "Read the reminders back to me" and "Change the evening one to nine o'clock."

Podcasts and audiobooks are stories and talks you listen to instead of read. Each podcast has episodes, and each audiobook has chapters. The player remembers where you left off, so you can start again later. People change how they listen: "Play it faster," "Go back thirty seconds," or "Skip to the next chapter." A grandfather may like a slow speed, so he says, "Slow it down a little." Some people swipe the screen to move on, but others just talk and say, "Next episode." Many players are automatic and start the next episode alone. If you do not want that, say, "Stop after this one."

Someone wants the current score of the football match, because their stream keeps freezing and the pizza is in the oven.
Score?
what's the score right now
Who is winning the match?
Has the game started yet? It's meant to kick off before lunch on Sunday
Give me the latest result for my team
Tell me how Sunday's match is going, I'm busy before lunch
Could you please read me the score as soon as anything happens? I'll be cooking before lunch on Sunday and can't watch.

Someone wants to know how many days are left until a nice event, like a garage sale, and may want to reset the count later.
Days until the twelfth of March?
how long till March twelfth
Count down to the twelfth of March for me

name: parking_time_left
does: Tells you how many minutes are left on your parking ticket and warns you before it ends, so drivers who love a long lunch can come back to no fine.
inputs: the place where you parked, such as the apron in front of the bakery, your ticket time, and the size of your car, small, medium or large
people say:
- How long do I have on my ticket?
- Warn me before my parking runs out
- Am I still okay in this spot?
- Tell me ten minutes before I have to move the car
- I'm at the shops, how much time is left?
- Will I get a fine if I stay till two?

Layla got home after a night shift with sore shoulders and tired eyes. The morning sky was grey. She had an appointment with the physio at noon, and a long soak in the hot tub sounded wonderful. She dropped her bag, looked out at the garden and sighed. "Brr, that water must be cold as a lake. I want to get in before my appointment." The assistant understood. It started the heater on the hot tub and set the water to thirty-eight degrees. "It will be warm in about forty minutes," it said, and offered to tell her when it was ready. Layla made a cup of tea, put on a soft robe, and waited. When the assistant gave its message, she slipped into the warm water with a happy sigh.

Parking is about leaving a car in a safe place while you do something else. People look for a free spot, pay for the time, and watch how much time is left. On a hot day the street can bathe in sun, so many drivers look for shade. Many places let you upload a photo of your ticket or pay with a phone. People change their parking by saying, "Add another hour," "How much time is left?" or "Remind me ten minutes before it ends." A silent phone can be a problem, so a good reminder buzzes. They also ask, "Find a spot near the library" or "Where did I park?"

Delroy sat in heavy traffic with both hands on the wheel. The road was jammed for miles. "Play the next episode of my podcast about old trains," he said to the car. "But don't start from the beginning. I already heard the first half." The assistant found the spot where he had left off and began to play. Delroy let out a breath. At a red light, he tried to stretch his back against the seat. Then he said, "Make it a bit faster. I don't want to be late for the end." The assistant raised the speed a little, and the host's voice sped up. Delroy smiled. The cars did not move, but the story did, and the time passed quickly.

Isaac stood on a ladder in his shop, hanging a new sign above the door, when his phone buzzed. His sister was flying in from Lagos. He climbed down. "Is my sister's flight on time, and can you text her the gate number?" he asked. The assistant checked and said the plane was running late by forty minutes. There had been several delays that morning because of fog. It sent his sister a text with the new gate. Isaac thanked it. "Tell me again when it lands," he said. The assistant promised. Isaac went back up the ladder, finished the sign, and had time to sweep the floor before the customers came.

Notes are small written pieces to keep ideas from slipping away. Maybe it is a shopping list, a thought for work, or a voice note you said out loud. People use notes to find things later, like the cheese you wanted to buy or the number for the plumber. Notes change: "Add eggs to my list," "Find my note about the trip," or "Make that note shorter." If someone wants to estimate the cost of a party, they write the numbers down and ask, "Read it back." A clean list with no old items is easier to read, so they say, "Delete the done ones."

Aminata sat on her bed with her phone and typed to the assistant. "ok so what do i pack for the hills this weekend? i think it will drop to fifty degrees at night." The assistant made a packing list: a warm jacket, wool socks, a hat, a water bottle, a flashlight and a rain cover for the tent. "Check that the flashlight is working," it added. Aminata laughed. "Good idea. I also want to jump in the lake if it's not too cold." The assistant put a swimsuit and a towel on the list, and a note to ask the camp if swimming was allowed. Aminata ticked each item as she packed her bag. Then she texted her friends a photo of the list.

Thiago was a driver, and his shift started before the sun came up. He stood in the kitchen with a mug and made a face. "This coffee is too weak for this morning," he said, rubbing his eyes. The assistant understood he wanted it stronger. It told the coffee machine to make the next cup with extra beans and less water. Thiago opened the sugar jar and spooned in a little. "No need to rush," said the assistant, "it takes two minutes." He waited, patient now that he could smell it. The new cup was dark and rich. Thiago took a long sip, smiled, and said, "Now I can drive." Then he picked up his keys and went out to his truck.

Andre closed his laptop and then opened it again, because the kids were making noise. "Create a new folder on the computer called Trip," he told the assistant. Then his daughter waved a paper at him. "Wait, no. Call it Plane tickets instead," he said. The assistant renamed the folder. "Put the three files from my downloads in it," he added. It moved the files and told him the folder now held three items. Andre checked the screen and nodded. The battery was low, so he asked the assistant to dim the screen. When the folder was closed, he plugged in the charger and went to make the kids lunch.

inputs: the person's age, what they enjoy, your budget, and where you are, so the shops are near you
people say:
- What should I get my brother for his birthday?
- I need a present for my teacher, nothing expensive
- Any ideas for a ten year old who loves space?
- I care about my aunt, so help me pick something nice

Offices and errands are the little trips that keep life going: a visit to the post office, a stop at the bank, or picking up a parcel. People plan them so they do not waste time. They look up opening hours and see how long the line is. They change plans by saying, "Finish my bank visit before noon," "Remind me to pick up the keys," or "Move the post office to tomorrow." A heavy box may mean going by car. In an office building, someone might also report a dripping faucet and say, "Tell the building manager."

Someone with high hopes of getting a parcel today, who has set an alarm for the delivery, wants the assistant to connect to the tracking and say where it is.
Parcel tracking
Where's my parcel?
Track it
Has my package left the depot yet?
When will the delivery come today?
Check the status of my order
Could you look up my parcel for me? I'm waiting at home and need to know if I should go out.

Someone wants to share a large number of cookies between people, and to hear the answer again if they missed it.
Split 48 between 6 people
48 divided by 6?
If six people share forty-eight cookies, how many does each get?
How many each if 6 share 48
Divide 48 by 6 and repeat the answer

Could you work out how many each person gets? There are six people and forty-eight cookies, and they come after school today.

Someone who is angry that the milk ran out again wants it put on the shopping list on the kitchen console, so they can weigh up what else is running low.
Milk, list
Add milk
We're out of milk
Put milk on my list
Out of milk again!
Note that we need milk

Assistant: I can't say what is safe or best. I can tell you that half is about two thousand three hundred crowns each.
Person: That helps. Show me the rate again in the evening.
Assistant: Yes, I will tell you the rate tonight.

It's getting late and I can't tell if the middle is cooked

Sergei sat on a bench in the park while his twins played on the slide. One of them sneezed, and he wiped her nose. He felt nervous, because the school had said it might call. "Did the school call me?" he asked his phone. "And how many times?" The assistant said there were three missed calls and one voicemail. Sergei asked to hear the voicemail. It was the school nurse, saying the boys were fine and that practice had ended early. He let out a breath. Then he said, "Call my wife and put her on speaker, and make it twice as loud, the wind is strong." The assistant did, and soon his wife's voice came out clear. "We're at the park," he said, smiling.

Sabine was eating her cereal and texting with one hand when her throat began to hurt. It was sore and scratchy. "book me a doctor, not tomorrow morning, i have a test," she typed to the assistant. The assistant asked which doctor she usually saw. "Dr. Weber, the one near school." It looked up the opening hours and said the clinic closed at five today. There was a spot at four. "I don't want to miss math class either," Sabine added. The assistant checked her calendar and saw math ended at three, so four would work. It booked the visit and sent a reminder for half past three. Sabine put down her spoon, drank some water, and went to get her bag.

Aoife was chopping green onions when she remembered the big match. She wiped her hands on a towel and said, "Excuse me, could you please read me the football results from last night? I have been in the kitchen all day, and I would like to know how my team did before my family gets home." The speaker said it would deliver the scores right away. It read out three results in a calm voice. Her team had won two to one. Aoife smiled and felt her whole body relax. "Thank you," she said. Then she asked it to read the headlines about the local market too, and the assistant did. She kept on cooking while the news played.

Ravi, a grandfather, was cold in bed on Saturday night. The garden outside looked frozen. He told the phone, "Wake me at seven on Sunday, and please don't let me stay in bed any later than that." The phone set an alarm for seven in the morning on Sunday and said it was ready. Then Ravi asked, "How long will I sleep if I go to bed now?" It was ten o'clock. The phone said that if he slept until seven, he would get nine hours. Ravi nodded. He asked it to play a quiet rain sound for thirty-one minutes. The phone started the sound, and Ravi closed his eyes.

Someone who is careful about their house wants to know if the front door is locked, and they ask from their phone.
Is the front door locked?
front door locked?
Did I lock up?
I think I forgot the door, can you check it?
I'm a bit worried, is the door shut and locked?
Check the lock on the front door for me.
I earn more when I get to work early, so tell me quickly if the front door is locked.
Could you please tell me whether I locked the front door when I left? I am too far away to go back, and I won't be able to relax until I know.

Fatou was packing lunches when her phone buzzed. She said, "Read me the top news about the bank, please. I need to hear about the loan rates." The assistant started to give her the business headlines. "No, wait," said Fatou. "Not the bank. I mean the city council news." It was urgent, because the council was voting on the school bus routes that morning. The assistant stopped, changed the topic, and read three headlines from the local news. One of them said the vote would be at ten. Fatou listened while she zipped the lunch bags and called the kids to the door.

Ruta burned her hand on the stove. She was not good with phones, but she remembered the speaker on the shelf. "Hey assistant, burn help!" she said. The speaker told her to hold the burn under cool running water for ten minutes. It said not to use ice. Ruta was about to grab a frozen bag from the freezer, but she stopped. She bathed her hand in the cool water from the tap instead. After a while she asked, "Next step?" The speaker said to cover the burn loosely with a clean cloth, and to call a doctor if it blistered badly. Ruta did as it said, and her hand felt much better.

Someone wants to join a work call from their pricey new laptop.
Join my call.
Get me into the meeting.
Open the team call.
Is the nine o'clock meeting live yet? Put me in.
I'm about to lock up the office, can you start the call for me?
Hey, hop on the standup for me, I'm holding a carton of milk and can't reach the keys.
Could you please join the video meeting with my manager? I'm running late, I still have to lock my bike, and I don't want to miss the start.
Would you mind connecting me to the planning call? My hands are full and I'd like to listen in while I walk to the station.

A bike route is the path you ride from one place to another. Years ago, people drew their routes on paper with a pencil. Now an assistant can design a route for you in a few seconds. People change a few things about it: how far they want to ride, how fast they want to go, and whether they like flat roads or hills. They say things like "Make it shorter," "Keep it under twenty kilometers," or "Find me a flat way to the lake." On a crispy autumn morning, many riders ask for a long route. On a hot day, they ask for a short one with shade.

Someone wants the calendar to update because a meeting has to move to a later time.
Move my meeting later.
Push the three o'clock to four.
Can you try to shift my call with Dana to tomorrow?
I won't be out of the dentist by three.
The automatic reminder still says three, but the meeting is at five now, can you fix it?
Any chance you could slide the team meeting back by an hour?
I'm stuck in traffic and I'm going to miss my two o'clock.
Would you please move my lunch with Omar to Friday? Something came up at work, and I would like to let him know as soon as possible.

Would you mind switching on the heater in the hallway? The baby is sleeping nearby and I don't want her to get chilly.

Ravi had borrowed his sister's pasta recipe, and now steam was fogging up the kitchen window. His hands were covered in flour, and his phone sat on a clean towel. "Set a timer for ten minutes and read me the next step," he said. The phone started the timer and read out the step: stir the sauce and add a pinch of salt. Ravi stirred the pot, tasted it, and added the salt. When the timer rang, the phone read the last step, and he drained the pasta. His kids sat down at the table, and they said it was the best pasta he had ever made.

Martha was cooking soup for her uncle. He was outside mowing the lawn, and he would be hungry soon. She stirred the pot and asked her speaker, "Time left?" The speaker said there were eleven minutes left on the timer. Martha cut some bread and set the table. Then she asked, "Final step?" The speaker read it out: add fresh parsley, then turn off the heat. Martha did that and smiled. When her uncle came in, wiping his hands, the soup was hot and the table was ready. He said it smelled wonderful.
