Gabriela, a retired teacher, sat in her kitchen when she saw a small light glow near her front gate. She was a little worried. She said to her assistant: show me the front door camera and tell me if anyone walked down the road today. The assistant put the camera picture on her tablet. It said that only the postman and a neighbour had come by, and the glow was just a local street lamp turning on. Gabriela laughed and felt calm. Then she asked it to turn the alarm on for the night. The assistant said the alarm was on and all the doors were locked.

When you buy something online, a shop packs it and sends it to your home. You can track the package to see where it is and when it will come. People ask 'where is my parcel?', 'what time will it arrive?' or 'send it to my office instead'. If the soft toy you ordered is the wrong colour, you ask for a refund. When the delivery truck is close, the app tells you. If a person made a mistake, they can say 'close this order' or 'cancel it'. A new computer mouse or a pair of socks is handled the same way.

Nikola was cleaning the old fridge at the back of his shop. He had to unplug it, and the cold boxes were already heavy in his arms when he remembered what he needed. He typed fast to his phone: put heavy cream, eggs and butter on the shoping list. The assistant added the three items to the shopping list. It then sent him a short message: three items added. Nikola noticed the list was missing flour, so he asked the assistant to add that too. It did, and the list now showed four things. He plugged the fridge back in after he had wiped it, and put the phone in his apron pocket.

Bo was at the kitchen table with a laptop and a cold coffee. The laptop battery was low and the only wall socket was behind the sofa. Bo said to the assistant: open the folder with the school forms and tell me how much battery is left. The assistant opened the folder, which held twenty plain files with the kids' names. Then it said the battery was at nine percent. Bo moved the laptop to the sofa, plugged it into the socket and asked the assistant to track which forms were still not signed. It made a short list of three forms and said it would keep track until they were done.

Juliette sat down on her sofa and picked up the remote, but she did not know which button to press. She asked the television: please put on channel thirty-one, the one with the weather and the bus route news. The television changed to channel thirty-one, and the weather lady came on the screen. Juliette smiled. Then she said: now make it louder and lock the remote so the grandchildren do not change it. The assistant raised the sound and said the remote was locked. A straight line of rain showed on the map, and Juliette went to find her umbrella.

Eitan was home alone when the smoke alarm began to beep. He was a little scared, but he remembered the tip his mother had stuck on the fridge: talk to the assistant. He said: call Dad. Then he stopped and said: no, wait, call Mum, Dad is on a plane. The assistant said it would call Mum instead. When Mum answered, the assistant told her Eitan needed help. She asked him to go outside and say his address. The assistant checked that it was the correct address, and Eitan wrote the street name on his hand so he could tell the firefighters when they came.

Birthdays come once a year, and many people forget them. An assistant can remember dates, suggest gift ideas and remind you to send a card. A weekly look at the next two weeks helps you plan ahead. People say 'remind me of Anna's birthday', 'what gift for a ten-year-old?' or 'order a cake for Saturday'. Some gifts are things to eat, like chocolate, and some are fuel for a hobby, like paint for an artist. When plans change, they say 'move the reminder a week earlier' or 'pick something cheaper'.

A robot vacuum cleans the floor on its own, so people have more time. They set a schedule, like every day at noon when nobody is home, and tell it which rooms to do. If the battery runs low, it goes back to its base. People say 'clean the kitchen now', 'skip the bedroom today', 'try the hall again' or 'stop, I have visitors'. Mopping works the same way: you say how wet and how often. A person can ask it to start once the post is brought in from the mailbox and the shoes are put away.

I am busy getting the children ready for a party, and the buzzing keeps waking the baby. The assistant said it had turned off the hourly alerts until tomorrow morning. Naoki also asked it to play a quiet song for the baby. The assistant played a soft lullaby, and the baby went back to sleep while the family got ready.

Victor works in an office, and this Saturday afternoon he planned to paint the spare room at home. The evening before, he told his assistant: this Saturday afternoon, please run the air purifier in the spare room and open the window vent for an hour, because paint smells make me cough. The assistant set both for Saturday at one o'clock and said it would send him a note when the air was fresh again. Victor was pleased. On Saturday, the dim light in the room came on and the purifier started with a quiet hum. By the end of the day the smell was gone.

The assistant sent the page to the printer in black and white and told Rizal that one page was printing. Rizal also said: and no extra copies. The assistant printed only one. Rizal took the warm paper, fed Bruno first, and then went to the kitchen.

Amelie watched through the window as the soil began to breathe again after the dry week. When the ten minutes were over, the sprinkler stopped on its own, and she went back to her pot.

Nour was out on a run with frozen fingers, so she did not want to type a long text. She was training for a school trip to the mountains. She tapped her watch and said: track steps. The assistant started counting steps and said it was ready. Halfway round the lake she said: pace now. The assistant told her she was running at six minutes for each kilometre. She grinned, because it was faster than last week. Back home she asked it to save the run, and the assistant added it to her list for the week.

Most cars have a fuel gauge that shows how much petrol is left. It is there so you can plan a run to the shops without getting stuck. People change small things about their cars all the time. Some swap summer tyres for winter ones. Others ask the car to warm up before a drive on a cold morning. If your back is sore after a long trip, you might say, "Make the seat warmer" or "Tilt the seat back a little." For the tyres, people say, "Check the pressure" or "Put some air in the front ones." To remember where you left the car, you can say, "Save this spot," and later, "Where did I park?"

Divya was a cook, and her feet were tired after a long day. The robot mower in her garden kept stopping halfway across the grass. She said to her phone, "Why does my mower stop?" The assistant checked the mower and said the battery was low. Divya laughed. She would have to practice being patient with it. "Please charge it tonight, and start the weekly mowing again by the end of the week," she said. The assistant told the mower to charge until morning. Then it made a weekly plan for Saturday at nine o'clock. It said the lawn would be cut every Saturday from now on. Divya smiled and went inside to make dinner.

A sports app keeps scores, teams and training plans in one place. It is for knowing how your team is doing without watching every minute. People change a few things all the time. If the score alerts are too noisy, they say, "Mute the alerts for this game." If they want a friend to see the match times, they say, "Share the schedule with Tom." When the battery on a fitness band is low, they ask, "Remind me to charge it." Each match is one item on the list, so you can also say, "Remove that item" or "Move training to Thursday." Simple words are enough.

A sprinkler is for giving the grass water so that it stays green. Most people set it to run early in the morning, when it is cool. You can change how long it runs and on which days. Some people say, "Water the lawn for ten minutes," or "Skip the sprinklers tomorrow, it is going to rain." If the dog digs holes near the fence, you might ask for a little less water there. When neighbours talk about their lawns, they often say, "Turn the sprinklers off for the weekend." A smart controller understands these everyday words and changes the plan for you.

An air purifier cleans the air in a room. It is for people who sneeze a lot, or who live near a busy road. Most purifiers have fan speeds, and people change them often. Say you come home from the market and the room feels stuffy. You might say, "Turn the purifier up," or "Run it faster for an hour." At night people say, "Make it quieter." A plant on the shelf will not clean the air much by itself, so many people keep a purifier too. In a narrow room, one small machine is often enough. To save power, you can say, "Switch it off at eight."

Iris was a busy parent, and the kids were noisy in the back seat. She stopped at a red light and spoke to her phone. "Book a haircut for me on Friday and tell me when the dentist opens." The assistant found a free time at a quarter past four on Friday and booked it. Then it said the dentist opened at eight in the morning. Iris asked it to save the dentist's number, and it did. "Also, put a note in my calendar to call the front desk about Leo's checkup," she said. The assistant added the note. The light turned green, and Iris drove on, glad that she had not needed to look at the screen.

When you buy something online, the shop sends you a tracking number. It is for knowing where your parcel is and when it will come. People change delivery plans often. If you think nobody will be home, you can ask for a different day or a safe place. Some say, "Deliver it to my neighbour," or "Send it to the shop near my work." Delivery windows can be narrow, like between two and four. A new suitcase for a trip might need to arrive before the weekend, so people ask, "Where is my parcel?" or "Can it get here by Friday?" If an order is wrong, they say, "Send it back and give me my money back."

A home alarm is for keeping your house safe when nobody is there. Motion sensors notice movement, and cameras record it. When it gets dark, many cameras switch to night mode. People often forget to turn the alarm on before they leave, so they say, "Arm the alarm when I go out" or "Did I lock up?" Pets can set off sensors, so people say, "Ignore motion in the hallway at night." If a car engine starts in the driveway at a strange hour, you may want to know about it, so you say, "Tell me if the camera sees someone outside."

When you shop in another country, prices are in a different currency. An exchange rate tells you how much your own money is worth there. The rate changes every day, so a price can look cheap on Monday and dear on Friday. People ask, "How much is fifty euros in dollars?" or "What is the rate today?" On a humid holiday in a hot location, nobody wants to do sums by hand. Some phones flash the price in your own money when you point the camera at a sign. You can also say, "Show prices in pounds" to change what you see.

Olivia worked as a cook and had a short nap before her shift. She woke up with a weird thought: her sister's birthday was tomorrow! She grabbed her phone and typed in a hurry, "find a gift for my sister, her birthday is tomorow, under thirty dollars". The assistant showed three ideas. Olivia liked the blue scarf from a shop near her work. "Get that one," she said. The assistant booked a pickup time at the shop for five o'clock and added a reminder to Olivia's calendar. Then it asked if she wanted a card too. Olivia said yes, and she went back to sleep for ten more minutes.

When a pet goes missing on a street, neighbours put up notices and post in the local group. The notice is for finding the animal fast. People change these notices as news comes in. They might say, "Add a new photo," or "Increase the area to the next street." A sharp reminder works well, like "Post it again at six, when people leave work." The notice might also be pinned at the cafe on the corner, and the local group can send an alert. When the pet is found, people say, "Take the post down and say thank you to everyone."

Dmitri was an office worker. He was walking across the big field behind his building when his phone beeped. The storage was almost full. He was about to go on a trip to the west coast and wanted room for photos. "Free up half of my storage," he told the phone. The assistant looked at what was taking up space and said old videos used the most. It offered to move them to the cloud. Dmitri said yes. Next he asked it to pack his ticket and hotel papers into one folder for the trip. The assistant did that too. Now the phone had twice as much free space.

Eilidh was tired after her night shift. In the white light of the car park she whispered to her phone, "How long to get home?" The assistant said the drive was thirty minutes, but traffic on the main road made it ten minutes longer than usual. "Find a faster way," said Eilidh. The assistant showed a route through quiet streets that was five minutes shorter. She also asked it to remind her to switch on the humidifier when she got home, because the flat felt dry. The assistant set a reminder for when she arrived. Eilidh started the car and followed the new route.

The assistant switched off the heater. Then it said she had used eight units so far, which was more than yesterday. It said the heater was the biggest part. Beatriz asked it to remind her to turn the heater down before she left next time.

Social media is a place where people post photos and short notes, and see what their friends are doing. Likes show that others enjoyed a post, and followers are people who want to see what you share. Notifications tell you when something happens. There can be too many, so people say, "Mute the alerts at night" or "Only tell me when my sister posts." Say you take a photo of your cereal bowl on a damp Monday morning. You might say, "Post this picture, but only for friends." Later, "Take it down" removes it.

Sara did not like gadgets. Her electricity bill was high, and she did not know why. A neighbour told her to ask the speaker. So Sara said slowly, "Can you tell me how much electricity I use?" The assistant said her house used a constant amount all day, even at night. It measured the fridge, the old freezer in the garage and a charger for her son's electric motorcycle. "The charger is on all night," it said. Sara asked it to switch the charger off every night and turn it on early on Thursday, when her son wanted to ride. The assistant made the plan. Sara smiled and said thank you.

name: world_clock
does: Says what time it is in another city, so a sudden phone call does not wake someone up when their blind is down and the room is dark.
inputs: the name of a city or country (no need to dust off an atlas)
people say:
- What time is it in Tokyo?
- Is it too late to call my brother in Canada?
- Are they awake in Sydney now?
- Time in Lagos
- How many hours ahead is Berlin?

Person: Remind me about my cousin.
Assistant: What should I remind you to do, and when?
Person: Pick her up at the airport. Her plane lands at four, and I want to chill for a while after I close the shop, so remind me one hour before.
Assistant: Done. I will remind you at three to pick up your cousin. Do you want a second reminder?
Person: No, but the roads are usually full on Fridays. Can you make it half an hour earlier?
Assistant: Yes. I will remind you at half past two instead.
Person: Thank you.
Assistant: You are welcome.

A watering timer is for giving plants water when you are busy. It turns the sprinkler on at the same time each day. People change the plan with the weather. In a hot week they may say, "Water the garden twice a day." Before a rainy day, they say, "Skip the next watering." Some systems warn you if the soil is too dry, and you can ask, "Tell me when the tomatoes need water." A small change in time can matter too, so people say, "Move the watering to six in the morning." Seeds need less water than big plants.

name: start_focus_timer
does: Starts a timer for focused work and makes the screen flash when it is time for a break.
inputs: how many minutes to work, how many minutes to rest, and what the break is for, like a crispy snack or a call to your father
people say:
- Let me work for twenty-five minutes, then tell me to stop
- Start a study timer
- I need an hour of quiet work
- Time me, then give me a five minute break
- Keep me on task for half an hour

Fiona did not trust the new thermostat. The screen was small and the buttons were confusing. One cold morning she said to the speaker, "I don't want it hot all day, just warm when I get up." The assistant asked what time that was. "Half past six," said Fiona. It made a schedule: the heating would come on at six, reach twenty degrees by half past, and go down by ten percent during the day. Fiona liked a soft, warm room in the morning, and not a hot one at noon. She thanked the assistant and went back to bed for a few minutes.

Rahul was seven years old and a little afraid of the dark hallway. Before bed he said to the speaker, "Lights on." The hall light came on. "Dimmer," he said, and it became softer. The heater in his room clicked on, and the assistant said the room would be warm soon. Rahul wanted to put his teddy to bed first, so he tucked the bear under the blanket. Then he got in himself and said, "Night light." The assistant turned on the little blue lamp and switched off the hall light. Rahul closed his eyes.

Many homes have a filter that needs changing now and then, like the one in a heater or a cooker hood. A filter is for keeping the air or the water clean and the machine working well. If a pipe leaks or a filter is dirty, you book a repair. People say, "Find a plumber for Tuesday," or "Remind me to change the filter every three months." Some ask for a visit in the middle of the week. Instructions often tell you to fold the old filter before you throw it away. If you have a long list, you can say, "Make a list of repairs for the house."

A restaurant booking holds a table for you at a certain time. It is for avoiding long waits, especially on the weekend. People change bookings often. They say, "Move my table to eight," or "We are five now, not four." If the group is smaller, they reduce the number. Menus show prices, and at the end the total on the bill is what you pay. For takeaway, people ask, "Is the kitchen open?" or "What time do you close?" To cancel, they say, "Cancel my booking."

Anil owned a small shop near an old factory. In the afternoon the sun came through the front window and made the shelves too hot. He spoke to his assistant. "Could you please close the blinds on the window side, because the sun is hurting the chocolates and I do not want them to melt?" The assistant lowered the blinds by half. Anil asked it to reserve that setting for every afternoon, and it saved the plan. The last thing he asked was to open the blinds again at five o'clock. The assistant said that was done.

A birthday reminder is for not forgetting a friend's special day. Phones can sync with your calendar, so dates from your contacts show up every year. People change these things. They say, "Remind me a week before Mum's birthday," so there is time to buy a gift. Gift ideas depend on the person: a card, flowers, or a picnic in the park. If a friend has a sore leg, a quiet dinner may be better than a long walk. You can say, "Find a gift under twenty dollars" or "Add a note to remember what she likes."

Person: Could you please help me with a word, because my son has a Spanish test tomorrow and we are trying to build a short word list over lunch?
Assistant: Happy to help. Which word do you want to translate?
Person: Smooth, like a smooth road.
Assistant: For a road, you say "liso." For things that feel soft, you say "suave." Shall I add "liso" to the list?
Person: Yes please. Can you also tell me what is on his whole test?
Assistant: Sorry, I can't see his school test. But I can quiz him on the list if you like.
Person: That would be great.

Pavel drove a delivery van all day. On his break he looked at his phone, because his grandma was visiting and he wanted dinner to be ready. "Turn the oven on to two hundred degrees and start the fancy coffee machine," he said. The assistant sent both commands to the kitchen at home. Grandma saw the oven light come on and soon smelled coffee. Pavel asked the assistant to make a note: dinner in forty minutes. Then he finished his sandwich and drove on, happy that she would not have to wait.

Francesca woke up with a sudden thought. Was the tax office closed on Fridays? She rubbed her eyes and said, "Could you please tell me when the tax office opens today, and how to get there, because I have to leave some papers before work and I do not want to wait in a long line?" The assistant said it opened at eight and that the walk took twelve minutes. It added the papers to her list. Outside, the snow had started to melt, so the assistant also told her to wear boots. Francesca got up and looked for them.

Tariq was a gardener. While he was trimming the hedge, he cut his hand with the shears. It was not a dangerous cut, but it bled a lot. He took out his phone with the other hand. "Cut hand. Help," he said. The assistant told him to press a clean cloth on the cut and hold his hand up. "Do not touch the cut with dirty hands," it said. After ten minutes the bleeding slowed down. The assistant asked if he wanted to call a doctor. Tariq said no, so it told him how to clean and cover the cut. It also said to skip his evening jog and rest.

On Tuesday, the air in Kai's flat felt dirty. Kai was a grandparent, and the heat from the radiators made the rooms dry and dusty. "Purifier on," Kai said to the speaker. The assistant turned on the purifier in the living room. After a while Kai asked, "Fan faster?" The assistant said it was now on high and the air was getting cleaner. It also offered to turn the purifier down at night so that it would be quiet. Kai said yes, and the assistant set it for ten o'clock.

A packing list is for making sure you bring what you need on a camping trip: a tent, a warm coat, food and a torch. Before leaving, people check the weather in the hills, because it can change fast. They change the list a lot. They say, "Add rain jackets," or "Take off the big tent, we are using the small one." Some families bring a kitten or another pet, so they say, "Put pet food on the list." A trip is more fun with delicious food, so they also say, "Add things for a campfire dinner." If you are not sure how to spell a place name, the assistant can help.

name: get_sports_results
does: Reads out the latest result of a team's match, such as a ball game last night, and says who won; it can connect to a live score feed and has a low-data mode.
inputs: the team name and the sport
people say:
- Did Arsenal win last night?
- What was the score in the cricket?
- How did my team do?
- Any football results from today?
- Who won the basketball game?

Kofi woke up early in a hotel in Lisbon. He expected a quiet morning, but he could hear a car engine outside. His taxi to the airport was coming at seven. "Could you please tell me how to say 'Please take me to the airport' in Portuguese, because it is important and the driver does not speak English?" he asked his phone. The assistant said the sentence slowly and spelled the hard words. Kofi said it back twice. Then he asked the assistant to save the phrase, and it put the phrase on his lock screen. He picked up his bag.

Lei woke up and the room was dim. She grabbed her phone and said, "Could you please check where my parcel is, because it is a toy for my nephew's birthday, and I will be out all day?" The assistant looked up the order and said it was out for delivery, with one stop left before hers. Lei asked it to leave the parcel with the neighbour, and the assistant sent that note to the driver. Then she said, "Please dim the lamp," and the assistant made it softer so she could sleep a few more minutes.

Person: I need to see the dentist.
Assistant: Which day would you like?
Person: Thursday. I am a bit scared of dentists, so please make it a quiet time.
Assistant: I understand. Mornings are usually quieter. Would ten o'clock suit you?
Person: Yes. The bus takes thirteen minutes, so that is fine. Should I bring my own toothbrush?
Assistant: I can't answer for the clinic, but I can add a note to call and ask. Would you like that?
Person: Yes, please.
Assistant: Your visit is booked for Thursday at ten, and the note is added.

The person wants the assistant to check for a water leak, because they were sweeping the kitchen and found a wet floor by a thick pipe.
Any leaks?
Check for a leak
Is water escaping anywhere?
The floor is wet, what is going on with the pipes?
Water is coming into contact with the wall, can you see if something is leaking?
Is the water meter running when nothing is on?
Could you please check the house for leaks, because I will be away for a week and I do not want to come back to a flood?
I think a pipe might be dripping, can you look into it?

The person wants the television sound to stay steady, so the adverts are not louder than the show; the volume is set once and kept flat.
Even out the sound
No loud adverts please
Stop the adverts being so loud
Keep the volume the same all the time
The ads blast my ears, can you do something?
I don't want to run for the remote when I already have my hat and coat on, so please keep the sound even
Turn on the volume leveller
Please make the shows and adverts equally loud, because the baby is asleep next door

Holiday lights are for making a home feel special. Many people use a timer or a light sensor, so the lights come on when it gets dark. The only thing you need to do is plug them in. People change them often. They say, "Turn the tree lights on at five," or "Boost the brightness a bit." For parties, they say, "Play holiday music in the kitchen." Traditions differ from home to home, but plans are easy to change, like "Move dinner to Sunday" or "Remind me to buy gifts on Friday."

Leo was new to the city and had a job interview in the morning. His old alarm clock was broken. After he finished ironing his shirt, he lay down with his head on the pillow and said to his phone, "Alarm six." The assistant set an alarm for six o'clock. "Quiet sound," Leo added, and the assistant picked a soft one. Then it asked if he wanted a second alarm, just in case. Leo said yes, ten minutes later. The assistant set it and said good night.

Elena was eight, and her class project was about teeth. She sat on the sofa with her mum's phone and said, "My tooth feels wiggly. I think the dentist should look at it." The phone asked which day she liked. "After school, when it's not raining," said Elena. The assistant found a free time at Dr. Rao's office on Thursday at four and booked it. The screen was very bright, and Elena squinted. "It's so bright in here," she said. The assistant dimmed the screen a little. Elena smiled. "That's fine," she said. The assistant read the booking back to her: Thursday, four o'clock, Dr. Rao. It also set a reminder for Thursday morning so she would not forget. Elena wrote the date on her project poster with a big green pen.

A nurse, home from a swim, wants the phone screen to be less bright.
make the screen dimmer
turn down the brightness
pls lower the brigthness
my eyes hurt, the screen is blinding me
Can you make the display a bit softer?
It's way too bright in here for my phone
Brightness down please
Could you please lower the screen brightness, because I'm lying in bed and my husband is trying to sleep?

A campsite booking is how you keep a spot for your tent. It makes sure there is room when you arrive, so you do not drive for hours and find a full field. People change a booking a lot. They say things like "move it to Saturday," "add one more night," or "make it for five people instead of four." Many sites ask you to pay when you book, and some let you pay when you get there. After a long walk, the best part is often a crispy breakfast cooked on a small stove outside the tent. If the weather turns bad, you can ask to cancel or to switch to another weekend.

Person: Can you book me a haircut and remind me the day before?
Assistant: Of course. Which day would you like the haircut?
Person: Friday morning, after I lock up the greenhouse.
Assistant: Is nine o'clock all right?
Person: Yes, nine is good. I want a soft trim, nothing short.
Assistant: Done. You are booked for Friday at nine, and I will remind you on Thursday.
Person: Can you also invite my brother and tell him the time?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't send invitations to other people. I can book a second chair next to yours, if you like.

name: check_room_air
does: Scans a room for dust, smoke and stale air and says whether the air is smooth and fresh or stuffy.
inputs: which room, and the month if the person wants a pollen check, like April
people say:
- Does it smell stuffy in here?
- Is the air okay in the bedroom?
- My nose is itchy, is it the dust?
- How is the air in the kitchen after cooking?
- Should I open a window?

Reading text aloud is a feature that lets a phone speak the words on its screen. It helps people who find small print hard to see, and people who just want to listen while their hands are busy. Changing it takes quick, simple words. People say "read this to me," "talk slower," "make the text bigger," or "stop reading." Some want a different voice, and some want the phone to look at a page and read it all the way to the end. The length of the text does not matter much, because a short note and a long article both work. You can also ask it to read only one paragraph.

Meera was chopping onions in the noisy kitchen of the restaurant when her phone buzzed on the shelf. She wiped her hands and said, "Tell me if my parcel came today and remind me to pick it up from the post office on my break." The assistant checked the mail notice. It said the parcel was waiting at the post office on Elm Street. Then it set a reminder for two o'clock, which was when her break started. Meera also asked if the delivery date would change, and the assistant said it had not. "Thank you," said Meera. She turned the fan down so she could hear the reminder later and went back to her onions.

Ngozi had moved to the city in june, a few weeks after her baby Ada was born. A neighbour had lent her a baby monitor, but Ngozi had not learned how to turn it on. It was late, and she was holding Ada with one arm, so she typed with her thumb: "remnid me to feed ada in half an hour and put the monitor on". The assistant set a timer for thirty minutes. Then it switched on the monitor in the nursery and told her the sound was working. Ngozi sat down in the dark with Ada and watched the little green light on the phone. When the timer rang, she was ready.

Person: I'm having a party on Saturday and I need music.
Assistant: Nice! What kind of music do you want?
Person: Something perfect for dancing. Not too slow.
Assistant: Okay. How many songs should I put in the playlist?
Person: Double what I had last time. I wrote it down with a pen, but I lost the paper. I think it was thirty.
Assistant: Then I will make it sixty songs. Do you want the volume to rise as the guests arrive?
Person: Yes, can you make it rise slowly?
Assistant: I'm sorry, I can't change the volume on a schedule. I can start the playlist quietly, and you can turn it up when the room fills.

Eun-ji woke up on Saturday with a jump. Her sister's birthday dinner was that night, and she had no gift. She grabbed her phone from the pillow, still half asleep, and said, "Gift ideas." The assistant asked who the gift was for. "My sister. She likes plants," said Eun-ji. The assistant gave three ideas: a small fern, a fancy watering can and a book about herbs. Eun-ji liked the watering can. Then she asked the assistant to put "buy a card" on her list for the afternoon. She told no one about the plan, so the secret did not leak, and at the dinner her sister was the only guest who was surprised.

Omar had moved to the city a week ago and knew almost nobody. One night he lay in bed, tired, with a book on his phone. He said, "Could you please play my audiobook from where I stopped? I fell asleep last night, and I missed the end of the chapter." The assistant found his place in chapter nine and began to play. The story was about a girl on a long swim across a cold lake. The screen was bright, so Omar asked the assistant to dim it, and it lowered the light. The narrator's voice felt close and calm in the quiet room. When Omar stopped answering, the assistant paused the book and saved his place.

Lucy sat in her kitchen with her phone on the table. Her granddaughter lived in Switzerland, where it was snowy, and Lucy wanted to send her a rose bouquet from a shop there. "How much is a hundred francs in dollars?" she asked. Then she laughed. "Oh, no. I meant pounds, not dollars. I live in England, I don't know why I said dollars." The assistant looked up the exchange rate and said that a hundred francs was a little less than a hundred pounds. Lucy wrote the number on a note. "Remember the rate for me, please," she said, and the assistant saved it to her notes before she went to order the flowers.

name: quiet_sender
does: Stops mail from a frequent sender from landing in the inbox and drops it into a folder instead.
inputs: the sender's name or address (it could be a husband, a shop or a club), and the folder
people say:
- Stop the shop emails from showing up in my inbox
- I get too many mails from the gym
- Send everything from Pedro to the newsletter folder
- Those daily deals are driving me crazy
- Can you hide emails from that club?

name: plan_walk_route
does: Plans a walk or run of the right length and tells you if it is going to snow, so you do not get bored of the same old loop.
inputs: where to start (like the train station), and how long or how far
people say:
- I want a different run today
- Somewhere new to walk, thirty minutes
- The same loop is boring me
- A route from the station that is about five kilometres
- Where can I go for a walk with the dog?

Nora sat at her desk with a cold coffee in one hand. Her video call kept freezing, and her boss was talking about the end of the quarter. She typed with her other hand: "wifi is so slwo, can you restart the router". The assistant said it would restart the router, and it did. The little lights on the box went dark and then came back one by one. After about a minute, the assistant told her the wifi was working again. Nora tried the call again, and this time the picture stayed sharp. It was fast enough for her boss's slides to load without any stops. She thanked the assistant and finished the meeting.

Mariam got home from the hospital at seven in the morning after a long night shift. She was cold and tired. She carried a bag of groceries into the kitchen and put down a bottle of orange juice. "Tonight after dinner, make my bedroom warmer by several degrees," she said to the thermostat. The assistant asked how warm she wanted it. "About twenty-one," said Mariam. The assistant set the heating for the evening, and it turned the radiator in the hall down so no heat was wasted. Then Mariam drank her juice, drew the curtains and slept all day. When she woke up, the bedroom was nice and warm.

Person: I forgot how tall I am in feet. I am 140.
Assistant: 140 what? Centimetres?
Person: Yes, centimetres.
Assistant: That is about four feet seven.
Person: Is a cow taller than me?
Assistant: A cow is usually about 140 to 150 centimetres tall at the shoulder. So it is about the same as you, or a little more.
Person: Wow. Thank you!
Assistant: You're welcome. It was nice of you to ask so politely, and I hope the farm trip is fun.

A world clock tells you what time it is in other cities. It is for people who call family far away or who work with teams in different places. Before a call, you might say "what time is it in Tokyo?" or "is it too late to ring Mum in Lima?" People also change the clock itself: "add Sydney," "show me London and Cairo," or "move my alarm back one hour." A rough rule is that each step across the map is about an hour. If you want to schedule a meeting, check that the hour works for everyone. Mail in a mailbox is collected at local time, and calls are too.

Beatrice was cooking beans on the stove when hot water splashed onto her hand. It hurt, but her roommates were asleep, so she whispered to her phone, "My hand got burned. I don't want a long video, just tell me what to do." The assistant answered in a quiet voice. It told her to hold the burn under cool running water for ten minutes. It said not to use ice, butter or toothpaste. Then it asked if the skin had blisters, and she said no. The assistant told her to cover the burn with a clean cloth and to call a doctor if it got worse. Beatrice turned off the stove and held her hand under the tap.

Haruto was seventy-two and needed a new switch for the lamp in his hall. He sat with his tablet and said, "I want to order a light switch, a plain white one, and have it come on the first of May." The assistant showed him three switches. One was very expensive, with a little screen on it, and Haruto laughed. He picked the cheapest white one. The assistant ordered it and chose the first of May for delivery. It also reminded him to disconnect the power at the main box before changing the old switch. Haruto wrote "turn off the power first" on a sticky note and put it on the lamp.

Sabine had taught maths for forty years, and now she was in her kitchen waiting for her grandchildren. The shop had shipped her a new router last week, but the old wifi still kept dropping with constant stops. She typed with two fingers, fast and without capitals: "guest wifi pasword for the kids". The assistant made a guest network with a short password and read it out slowly: two words and four numbers. It also said that the guests could not see her files. Sabine wrote the password on a card and put it on the fridge. When the children arrived, they connected in a minute, and Sabine made tea.

A parent wants to know how warm the sea is for a young child, since there is no heater at the beach to warm up by and the midday sun can burn.
Sea temperature?
How warm is the water today?
Is the sea cold right now?
Can the kids swim without freezing?
What's the water like at the bay at the moment?
I'm taking the little ones down later, is the water warm enough?
How cold is it in the sea?
Could you please tell me the water temperature at the beach, because my daughter is only four and gets cold very fast?

does: Opens or locks the pet door so a pet can go out in the sunshine but is stopped from leaving at night.
inputs: which pet door (like the left one at the back), whether it should be open or locked, and the time
people say:

- Let the cat out in the morning
- Lock the dog flap at ten
- I want the dog to stay in while I'm at work

I'm in the rain with my hands full, so could you please read me the main stories, because I can't scroll my phone?

Text messages are short notes you send from one phone to another. A group chat is a text with many people in it, like a family planning a pizza night. People use texts to ask questions, share photos and reply later when they are busy. To change how texts work, they say things like "read my messages," "reply that I'm on my way," "mute this chat," or "send the first one again." If the order needs a total, someone might type "how much is it all together?" Some phones read new messages aloud, which helps when your hands are full, and they let you answer by talking.

Thu was a cook, and guests were coming to her flat in an hour. She was in the kitchen, stirring a pot, when she remembered that she had lost her necklace behind the sofa. "In an hour my friends come," she said to the speaker. "Make the living room lights brighter, and tell me when it is half past six." The assistant raised the ceiling lights to full. Thu found the necklace under a cushion and laughed. Then she asked for warmer light, because the white glare did not show the true colour of the food. The assistant changed the lamps to a soft yellow, and she was happy. She still had time to vacuum the rug.

A person wants the slow wifi fixed or checked, because it is giving them less speed than usual.
The internet is crawling
Videos keep freezing
Pages take forever to load
I try to open anything and it just spins
I can't even post a photo, something is wrong with the wifi
Is the connection broken?
It's been like this all morning and nothing loads
Something's off, my phone is barely working at home

Bjorn was sixteen and texting his friends in the family room when he noticed the electricity bill on the table. It looked high. He picked up his phone and typed, "How much less power did we use this month than last month?" The assistant looked at the home energy numbers and said they had used about half as much as in winter, thanks to the new solar panels. Bjorn was happy. "Post a picture of that graph in the family chat," he said, and the assistant did. Then he put his dad's hammer back in the drawer, since he had been fixing the bike earlier, and went to eat dinner.

A person with a blender in a shopping bag wants the next train going north, and does not want a bus.
Next train north, not a bus
No buses, just trains going north

Can you check the trains going up north?
Not the bus please, I'd like a train north, and I want to get home while the sun still shines
What's the quickest way north that doesn't involve a bus?

A video is a moving picture that you record on your phone and watch later. People use videos to remember things, like a trip to visit grandparents or a clip of a cat chasing an orange across the kitchen. After you record a clip, you can share it with a friend or send it to a family chat. People change things with short requests: "trim the end," "make it shorter," "play it again," "send this to Dad," or "save it to my phone." If something is urgent, such as a clip that must reach someone before a deadline, they say "send it now."

A person wants the final score of last night's round of the cup, which they missed while eating apple pie on a cool evening.
Who won last night?
Score?
What was the final score of the match?
Did we win?
Tell me how the game ended
How did my team do?
What happened in last night's game?
I fell asleep before the end of the game, so could you please tell me the final score? My friends will ask me about it at work tomorrow.

A person wants to double a cookie recipe for a quiet party in January.
Double this recipe
Make it twice as big
I need twice as much dough
Can you make this for twelve instead of six?
Help me build a bigger batch from this cookie recipe
I want 24 cookies, not 12
How much flour do I need if I make twice as many?
Please double all the amounts, because more people are coming than I thought

name: camp_night_check
does: Says how cold the night will get at a campsite, based on the recent weather and the expected fall in temperature, so campers know what to pack if the air will chill.
inputs: the campsite or place, the date, and how high up it is
people say:
- Will it be freezing at the campsite on Saturday night?
- Do I need a thicker sleeping bag?
- How cold does it get up at the lake at night?
- Should I bring a warm jacket for the hills?
- What's the weather like for our tent trip this weekend?

Baking bread takes time, and the oven timer helps. The dough must rise first, and then it bakes. People set the timer and change it with short requests: "ten more minutes," "make it fifteen," or "turn the heat down." To check a cake, you push a thin stick into the middle. If it comes out clean, the cake is done. If the top is getting dark too fast, you close the oven door and lower the heat. A busy driver who bakes late at night might say "remind me when the bread is done," because the timer is the only thing keeping the loaf from burning.

A short video can show how to do a small job at home, like how to change a toothbrush head. People also record clips when something good happens: a baby's first steps, a dog that comes running, or a quick tour of a new flat. They watch them later on a phone or a television. To change what a video does, they say "pause," "go back ten seconds," "turn on the words," or "make it louder." When the family gets back from a trip, they often say "play the clips from the beach" or "share the video with Grandma." Home videos are mostly for keeping memories.

name: order_takeaway
does: Orders food from a restaurant and sends it to your door, so nobody has to lose an evening in a queue.
inputs: the restaurant (like the noodle place up the hill), the dishes, and the home address
people say:
- Get me the usual from the Thai place
- I'm too tired to cook, order something
- Send two pizzas to my flat
- Dinner for four, delivered by seven
- Can you get that burger place to bring food here?

Person: My room smells funny.

Time zones are the reason a podcast you love can come out at a different hour for you than for the host. When it is noon where you live, it may be night in another country. A clock app shows these differences, and people use it to check the time before a personal call. They say "what time is it in Berlin?" or "show me Delhi next to my city," or "wake me at eight, my time." When you travel, the phone usually changes to the new zone on its own. If it looks wrong, you can say "set my clock to local time." A short report of the time is often all you need.

A person wants to know how many medium boxes are needed to pack a flat, since only a phone charger is packed so far.

Number of boxes for a two-bedroom place?

An inbox is the place where new emails land. People use it for letters from work, shops and friends. A busy inbox gets messy, so people ask for small changes: "show me only unread mail," "move this to the trip folder," "delete the old ones," or "attach the photo." If a message is about an expensive purchase, they may say "mark it important." Sometimes a short email is not the best way, so people text instead. But long details, like a trip plan with times and addresses, fit better in an email, because they stay in one place and can be found later.

A person wants a room near the station for two nights, with a cooked breakfast.

Anil had taught history for thirty years, and now he sat in a restaurant with old friends. The dinner was cooked and nearly ready, but he saw that his everyday account was low. He leaned over his phone and said, "Excuse me, could you please move a hundred pounds from my savings to my checking account? I'd like to pay the bill for everyone tonight." The assistant asked him to confirm. "Yes, a hundred," he said. It checked the setting for transfers between his own accounts, moved the money, and told him the new balance. Anil guessed the bill would be eighty, and he was right.

Sylvie had a long day at the office, and her coffee was stale on the desk. She plugged in her laptop and said to her phone, "Move my meeting with Tom to Tuesday at two. No, wait, Wednesday at two." The assistant moved the meeting to Wednesday and sent Tom a note about the new time. Then Sylvie remembered the slides. "Upload the slides to the meeting too," she said. The assistant attached the file to the calendar event so everyone could open it. Sylvie checked the screen. Wednesday at two, with the slides. She nodded, finished her cold coffee and went home.

Hodan drove a taxi, and on Wednesday his shift would begin at six. He was hungry and had only a few minutes at the red light. He said to his phone, "Order a chicken wrap from the place on Main Street. No, make that the falafel wrap." The assistant changed the order to a falafel wrap. It asked if he wanted the flat bread or the regular one, and Hodan said flat. The assistant set the delivery for half past five, at his front door. Then it asked about a tip, and he chose ten percent. When the light turned green, Hodan drove on, happy that dinner was coming.

Mia was at a cafe with her friends, and she had written the party plans on a napkin. Her friend Zoe had passed her exams, and they wanted to celebrate. Mia said to her phone, "Text Zoe that we are meeting at six at the pizza place. Don't put any emojis in it, please." The assistant wrote the message with no pictures, only words, and showed it to Mia. She read it, then asked to add "bring your sister." The assistant added the line at the bottom of the message and sent it. Zoe replied right away. Mia put the napkin in her pocket.

Bo was not good with technology. He had a work deadline on Friday, and every time his phone lit up, the messages from his sister showed on the screen where his coworkers could see them. Bo held the phone up to the speaker on his desk and said, "Everybody in this office can read my phone. It's getting hot in here with all these eyes on me." The assistant understood. It turned off message previews on the lock screen and said, "Done. Now your messages will only say that you have a new message. Nobody can read the words unless you unlock the phone." Bo still looked unsure, so he asked it to play a short sound to prove it worked. A test message came in. The phone played a soft chime, and the screen only said new message. Bo smiled and went back to his work.

Nadia was eight, and she was playing a shop game with her cousin. A toy cloud pillow cost sixty pesos in the game, and she wanted to know what that was in dollars. She said to the tablet, "Hey, how much is sixty pesos in dollars?" The assistant looked up the exchange rate and said, "Sixty pesos is about three dollars and fifty cents today." Nadia wrote the number down on her paper. Then she asked the assistant to select the rate for euros too, because her cousin liked to pretend he was in Paris. The assistant showed both rates on the screen. "That's fine," said Nadia. "Now we can play." The assistant told her that rates change every day, so the numbers might be a little different tomorrow.

When you park in a city, you often pay for the time you stay. Some meters have a button for more minutes, and many people use a phone app instead. The app shows how much time is left and can send a quick warning before it ends. If you need longer, you can say, "I need thirty more minutes" or "Give me more time." If you leave early, you can say, "Stop my parking" or "Remove the extra time." People also ask, "Where is the closest free spot?" or "How long have I got left?" The assistant looks at the timer, changes it, and tells you the new end time so you do not get a ticket.

Bram was a grandfather who loved old films. One rainy afternoon he spoke to the speaker in his living room. "Excuse me, could you please tell me what is playing at the cinema in town this weekend? My granddaughter is visiting from her office job in the city, and I would like to take her somewhere warm and dry inside." The assistant named three films and their times at the cinema on Main Street. Bram asked it to note the Saturday afternoon comedy in his calendar. The assistant said, "I have noted it. Saturday at 2:30." Then it offered to play the trailer. Bram said yes, and he and his granddaughter watched the little clip on the phone, laughing at the funny parts.

A power cut can happen in a big storm, or when a tree falls on a wire near the ocean. It is important to be ready. Most people keep a torch and a radio in a drawer. Many also hold on to a small battery that keeps the internet box running for a while. When the lights go out, people ask the assistant, "Is there a power cut on my street?" or "When will the lights come back?" They might say, "Turn on the phone light" or "Call the power company." In a real emergency they say, "Call for help" or "Phone the fire department," and the assistant dials the number and keeps the line open.

Print the file and use the front and the back of the page

Zeynep worked in an office, and her lawn grew fast in the spring. One evening she said to her phone, "Set the robot mower to cut the grass half as short as last time. It was too close to the dirt." The assistant raised the blade height. It said, "I raised the cutting height by half an inch. The mower will run tomorrow at nine." Zeynep also asked the assistant to organize the week so that the mower would run on Monday, Wednesday and Friday instead of every day. The assistant changed the plan and read it back to her. Then she asked it to keep the mower away from the ring of flowers by the old tree. The assistant drew a small no-go circle on the map and said it was done.

Natasha was a retired teacher, and she wanted her hair cut before her niece's wedding. She sat on her porch with her tablet and typed fast: "book me a haircut tomorow at ten at the salon on Elm Street". The assistant found the salon, saw that ten o'clock was free, and booked it. It wrote, "Your haircut is booked for tomorrow at 10:00 with Lena." Natasha, who was tall and always stood very straight, said she would love to have the same time next month too. The assistant checked and said that the salon did not take bookings that far ahead yet. It offered to remind her in three weeks to try again. Natasha said that would be lovely.

Juliette was late for work and her phone was almost dead. She ran past the kitchen and called out, "I keep forgetting the salad for the party tonight!" The assistant understood. It put "buy salad" on her to-do list for after work. Juliette was already at the door when she said, "My list is a mess, and the meeting is first." The assistant moved the meeting to the top. Then it offered to push each unfinished task to tomorrow. Juliette said yes, and the assistant moved the three tasks she had not done and told her what was left for today. She grabbed her bag and left, a little less worried.

The person is wet from the rain, will hang up the coat, and wants the kettle on for tea, not a can of soda.
Kettle on

Start boiling water for tea
I'm soaked and I need something warm

Could you switch on the kettle? I'm making tea for the whole family.
Heat up some water, I want a hot cup of tea
Tea time!

A small burn or a cut happens to almost everyone. First aid is what you do before a doctor can see it. For a small burn, you hold the skin under cool water for a long time, about ten minutes. For a cut, you press a clean cloth on it. People who go on a long march or hike often carry a small kit with bandages. An assistant can make the steps easier to follow. People say, "How do I treat a burn?" or "Show me what to do for a cut." They also say, "Set a timer for ten minutes" while the burn is under the water. If it looks serious, they say, "Call an ambulance."

Nathan had just woken up. The sun was bright and his head felt heavy. He mumbled to the smart speaker, "Unlock the front door and tell me if anyone came by last night." The assistant unlocked the door and said, "The door is open. The camera saw one person at nine, a delivery driver who left a box on the step." Nathan yawned. He had slept the whole night, and now he wanted a bath. He went outside, picked up the box, and saw that it had split along one side. Back inside, he asked the assistant to lock the front door again. It did, and said, "The front door is locked."

Baraka was a busy parent with a baby who woke up every night. At two in the morning, Baraka said quietly to the baby monitor, "How much did she drink today? I think she wanted double at the last feeding." The assistant looked at the feeding log. It said, "The total today is five bottles. The last feeding was twice as big as the one before." Baraka asked it to measure the room temperature too. The assistant said it was 68 degrees, which was fine for a baby. Baraka nodded and asked for a reminder about the next feeding at five. The assistant set it and said goodnight in a soft voice.

Assistant: Okay. I will remind you at the end of your shift.

A recipe says how much food to use for a certain number of people. Sometimes you need more or less. If a cake recipe makes eight slices and you only have four guests, you can cut every amount in half. Many people ask the assistant to do this work. They say, "Make this recipe for six," "Cut the recipe in half," or "Double the sugar and the flour." They also ask, "How many tablespoons are in a quarter cup?" The cooking time may change too, because a smaller cake bakes faster. Black pepper and salt are tricky, so people often taste first and ask for a little more.

Phone calls are for talking to someone when you cannot visit them. Most phones keep a list of the people you called and the calls you missed. If you miss one, a voicemail may be waiting for you. People say, "Call Mum," "Phone the dentist," or "Who just called me?" They say, "Put it on speaker" when their hands are busy, like when they push a shopping cart or stir a creamy soup. If they cannot guess who called, they say, "Call back the last number." To hear a message, they say, "Play my voicemail." The assistant finds the number, starts the call and tells you when someone picks up.

Person: Next chapter.
Assistant: Which book would you like to continue? You have two open, the mystery and the garden book.
Person: The mystery. Only ten minutes, please.
Assistant: Okay, ten minutes. Shall I read it aloud or just open it on the screen?
Person: Read it aloud. I'll brush my teeth while I listen. My ear is sore from the headphones, so use the speaker.
Assistant: Using the speaker. Starting chapter eleven. I'll stop in ten minutes.

Person: I cut my hand on the shears. What do I do?
Assistant: Is it bleeding a lot, or is it a small cut?
Person: Small. Actually no, it's deeper than I thought.
Assistant: Press a clean cloth on it and hold your hand up high. If the bleeding doesn't stop in ten minutes, you need help. Do you want me to call someone?
Person: Yes, call my wife. Wait, call my neighbor instead. My wife is driving.
Assistant: Calling your neighbor now. I'm saving this note so you can show the doctor.
Person: Thank you. I was in a rush with the electric hedge trimmer.
Assistant: Please unplug it and sit down until your neighbor comes.

A sprinkler gives your garden water so you do not have to carry it by hand. Most are set for certain days and a time of day, often early in the morning. People change how long it runs, which days it works, and which part of the garden gets water. They say, "Water the lawn for ten minutes," "Skip watering today, it's raining," or "Water the square bed by the fence twice a week." Some people carry a small soil meter in a pocket and ask, "Is the soil dry?" You can also watch the weather and say, "Tell me if it will rain tomorrow," so the water is not wasted.

Person: I need to book movers for Saturday.
Assistant: What time would you like them, and what is your new address?
Person: Nine in the morning. I have about fifteen boxes and a sofa. My dad is helping too.
Assistant: I can look for movers that are free on Saturday. Saturday is a busy day, so only one company has a slot at nine. Shall I book it?
Person: Yes, please. But I don't know my new street number yet.
Assistant: Okay, I'll hold the slot. Tell me the address when you have it.

Layla was a student waiting at the airport. Her flight to Lisbon seemed late, and many people were standing near the gate. She was holding a paper pot of noodles and almost let it fall when she took out her phone. She said, "What time does my flight leave? I don't want the old time, I want the newest one." The assistant checked the airline page and said, "Your flight is delayed forty minutes. It now leaves at 6:15 from gate 12." Layla was relieved, because she had thought it was cancelled. She asked the assistant not to tell her about the other flights, only hers. The assistant said it would warn her if the time changed again.

Amelie was a child who loved to walk. After a long walk with her dad, she looked at her digital watch and said, "Hey, how many steps did I do today? I think I did more than yesterday." The assistant said, "You did 8,400 steps today. Yesterday you did 6,100, so you did more." Amelie cheered. Her dad said they would buy meat for dinner on the way home, so Amelie asked for the shortest way to the shop. The assistant said, "Turn left at the park and walk ten minutes." Amelie held the phone out in front of her like a map, and they went off together.

The person wants the room cooler. It is rainy outside, but baking all morning has made the house too warm for a jacket.

The reporter said a truck had broken down ahead and the road would open soon. Eleanor sent her friend a short message to say she would be ten minutes late.

News is a short report about what happened today. Many people ask for headlines in the morning, for sports scores, or for news about their town. They say, "What's the news?" "Give me the sports results," or "Read me the weather and the local news." They can also change what they hear: "Less politics, more sport," or "Block stories about the election." Some people hold a phone in one arm while they make breakfast, so they ask the assistant to read the stories aloud. A tall stack of newspapers is not needed anymore, because you can just say, "Tell me what happened today."

Smart locks let you open the door without a key. They are useful when your hands are full, like when you carry luggage or a bag from the market. People say, "Lock the front door," "Is the back door locked?" and "Open the garage." A camera at the door can show who is there, say a person in a brown coat. You can give a code to a guest or a babysitter and remove it later. Parents may ask, "Tell me when the kids come home." Before bed, many people just say, "Lock everything." Even while you bathe the baby upstairs, you can ask whether the door is shut.

Bram worked in an office and he always forgot things. One chilly morning he told his phone, "Remind me at lunchtime to buy fifty stamps and a pound of coffee." The assistant said, "I will remind you at twelve o'clock." Bram took a breath and added, "And remind me when I get to the post office, not before." The assistant said it would send a reminder as soon as he arrived there. Later, a message popped up on his phone: "You are near the post office. Buy stamps." Bram laughed. He could breathe easier now, knowing nothing would be missed.

The tablet will stop at eight tonight." Her brother groaned. He wanted to watch a show about planes that fly over their town. Marisol offered him a bedtime story instead, and the assistant started one about a little cloud.

He asked the assistant to run the pump for three hours, and it set a timer. Then he went back to bed for a little while.

Measurements tell us how big, how heavy or how hot something is. In some places people use inches, pounds and degrees Fahrenheit. In others they use centimeters, kilograms and degrees Celsius. When you visit another country, the numbers can seem strange. A box of flour may be in grams, not cups. People ask, "How many centimeters is ten inches?" or "What is seventy degrees in Celsius?" or "Is a kilo more than two pounds?" A purple measuring cup with both kinds of lines can also help. The assistant gives you the answer in the units you know.

Baking turns dough into bread, cakes or cookies with heat. Dough needs time to rise, and it grows faster in a warm kitchen, like in August. When you see it double in size, it is ready for the oven. Every recipe has a baking time and a heat. People ask, "Set the oven to 350," "Start a timer for forty minutes," or "How long do cookies bake?" They may say, "Make it ten minutes shorter" or "Lower the heat a little." People often bake soft bread for a sick friend, and they ask the assistant to ring when the timer ends.
